articles.title: A finished model answering a request
articles.html:
Inference is running a checkpoint that is no longer being trained. A caller sends an input. A replica runs the model. The caller receives an output. Training already chose the weights. Your job starts when those weights have to answer real traffic.

Name the object you serve before you name the tool. A serving artifact is the weights, the tokenizer or processor, the config, and an eval that says this file may serve. A directory of training shards plus optimizer state is a resume point for the trainer. It is a different object. Loading it onto a serving machine moves bytes the server will not use, and the server still may refuse to boot.

Mechanism. A replica loads one digest into GPU memory, reserves space for requests that are in flight, and pulls work from a queue. For a language model the in-flight state is the cache of keys and values for tokens already seen. Replicas do not wait on each other. If one dies, the load balancer stops sending it traffic and the others keep answering. A training step is the opposite shape: every rank holds a piece of the same step, and the step finishes when the last rank finishes.

Worked numbers. A 7 billion parameter model in BF16 is 2 bytes per parameter.

7,000,000,000 × 2 bytes = 14 GB of weights.

Adam keeps two moments in FP32, 4 bytes each, so 8 bytes per parameter.

7,000,000,000 × 8 bytes = 56 GB of optimizer state.

The training directory in this example is about 14 + 56 = 70 GB before gradients: the BF16 weights and the two moments. A mixed-precision trainer that also keeps an FP32 master copy of the weights adds another 4 bytes per parameter, about 28 GB, and this 70 GB does not include it. The server wants the 14 GB. Copying this directory moves 70 / 14 = 5 times the weight bytes, and the shard layout is still wrong for the server.

What fails.

  • The rollout crash-loops because the file is a training checkpoint.
  • A latency number is quoted with no prompt length and no batch.
  • Cost is a GPU-hour with no count of tokens.
  • A training step time is treated as a serving latency.

What you do. Write three lines before you change a flag: the digest you intend to serve, the latency you owe, and the dollars per million output tokens you can spend. Then confirm a process can load that digest.

serve --model /registry/run-1842 --max-seqs 1 --dry-load

articles.title: The life of one request
articles.html:
Follow one chat request until the path is boring. The client sends a prompt. A gateway authenticates it and picks a replica. The replica tokenizes the text, runs the model, and streams tokens back. A log line records the queue wait, the time to the first token, and the time between later tokens. If you cannot point at those three clocks, you are debugging a feeling.

The request is not the model. The model is the function. The request is one call to that function, with a length, a priority, and a deadline. Two requests that share a replica still have their own clocks. A slow request can be waiting in a queue while the GPU is busy with someone else. That wait never appears inside a kernel profile of the other request.

Mechanism. Admission control decides whether this call may enter the queue. The queue holds calls the GPU has not started. The engine then groups waiting calls into a batch and runs them. Streaming sends tokens as they are produced, so the caller can paint the first word before the last word exists. A timeout on the client can fire while the replica is still working. The replica does not automatically know the caller left, unless the server watches the connection.

Worked numbers. A prompt of 1,000 tokens spends 200 ms to produce the first token. After that, tokens arrive every 40 ms. A 50-token answer therefore costs 200 + 49 × 40 = 200 + 1,960 = 2,160 ms from the server's point of view, if you start the clock at the replica. Add 30 ms of network and the caller sees about 2,190 ms. Quote the 200 ms and the 40 ms separately. Averaging them into one "latency" hides which stage you can still move.

What fails.

  • The client timeout is shorter than the answer you promised to generate.
  • Queue wait is folded into model time, so a kernel change is proposed for a full queue.
  • The trace starts after tokenization, so a CPU stall looks like a fast GPU.
  • Two callers share a number that belonged to only one of them.

What you do. Log four timestamps for every call: arrived, left the queue, first token, last token. The differences are queue, time to first token, and inter-token time. Open the stage whose difference moved.

# arrived_ms queue_ms ttft_ms itl_ms tokens
1719  40  200  40  50

articles.title: Prefill, then decode
articles.html:
A language model does two different jobs inside one request. Prefill reads the prompt and builds the cache. Decode then produces one new token at a time, reading that cache plus the weights. They share a GPU and they do not share a bottleneck. A change that speeds prefill can leave decode alone, and the reverse is also true.

Callers feel prefill as time to first token. They feel decode as the pace of the stream after that. A long prompt with a short answer is a prefill problem. A short prompt with a long answer is a decode problem. Mixing those two shapes into one average latency is how a fleet looks fine while one product is late.

Mechanism. During prefill the model attends over the whole prompt in a few large matrix multiplies. The arithmetic intensity is high: a lot of math per byte moved. During decode each new token is a thin multiply. The GPU loads a large weight matrix to produce a small result, then loads the growing cache. Decode is usually limited by memory bandwidth. Batching helps decode because one load of the weights can score many sequences. It helps prefill less, because prefill was already doing a lot of math per load.

Worked numbers. Weights are 14 GB. Memory bandwidth is 3,000 GB/s. The time to read the weights once is 14 / 3,000 = 0.0047 s, about 4.7 ms. If a decode step is bandwidth-bound at batch 1, you get about 1,000 / 4.7 ≈ 210 tokens per second from that GPU. A prefill of 1,024 tokens might finish in 80 ms because it reuses each loaded byte across many tokens of math. Those 80 ms are not 1,024 / 210 seconds. Do not forecast prefill with the decode rate.

What fails.

  • A long-prompt page is met with a decode-batch change.
  • A streaming-speed page is met with a prefill kernel change.
  • Capacity is planned with one tokens-per-second number for both stages.
  • The dashboard has a single latency with no split by prompt length.

What you do. Split every latency chart by stage and by length bucket. When time to first token moves, look at prefill and the queue. When the gap between tokens moves, look at decode, batch size, and bandwidth.

# length_bucket ttft_ms itl_ms
short   90    28
long    640   31

articles.title: The numbers on that request
articles.html:
Four numbers belong on a serving request: latency, throughput, memory, and dollars. Latency is a deadline for one caller. Throughput is how many callers you finish per second. Memory is whether the weights and the cache fit. Dollars is what you pay per useful output. A replica can win on one of these and lose on the others. The job is to say which one the product is buying.

Latency without a percentile is a story. Report p50 and a tail, and say whether the clock is time to first token or the full answer. Throughput without a shape is also a story. A replica that emits 2,000 tokens per second on one long decode is a different machine from a replica that starts 50 short requests per second.

Mechanism. The GPU has a finite memory and a finite bandwidth. Weights occupy a fixed block. The cache grows with concurrent sequences and with how long they are. When the cache reservation plus the weights exceed the device, the engine rejects new work or evicts old state. Throughput collapses before the device "runs out of compute," because the scheduler is protecting memory. Cost follows from how long the GPU stays reserved, divided by how much output you produced while it was reserved.

Worked numbers. The GPU costs $2 per hour. Decode produces 200 tokens per second.

200 × 3,600 = 720,000 tokens per hour.

$2 / 720,000 = $0.00000278 per token, which is about $2.78 per million tokens.

That price assumes the GPU stays busy at 200 tokens per second. If the same GPU averages 20 tokens per second because traffic is quiet, the million tokens cost about $27.80. The hardware price did not change. The utilization did.

What fails.

  • A tail latency is reported as a mean.
  • Throughput is quoted from a batch size production never reaches.
  • Memory is checked for the weights and not for the cache at the longest allowed prompt.
  • Cost uses a full GPU-hour against a replica that was idle most of the hour.

What you do. Publish the four numbers for the traffic you actually have: p95 time to first token, tokens per second at the real batch, bytes reserved at the max sequence length, and dollars per million output tokens at the observed utilization.

p95_ttft_ms: 280
tokens_per_s: 200
reserved_gb: 40
usd_per_mtok: 2.78

problems.title: Which file
problems.promptHtml: A 7B run finishes and leaves about 70 GB on disk: 14 GB of BF16 weights and 56 GB of Adam moments, in trainer shards. Serving is asked to boot that directory. The loss matches the eval you trust. Does the server want this directory, and which bytes should it receive instead?
problems.answer: no; an exported bundle near 14 GB of weights plus tokenizer and config, not the 56 GB of Adam state.

problems.title: Four clocks
problems.promptHtml: A call arrives, waits 40 ms in the queue, spends 200 ms to the first token, then emits 50 tokens with 40 ms between tokens. How long is the model busy producing the answer after the first token, and why is the queue a separate number?
problems.answer: 49 × 40 = 1,960 ms of decode after the first token; the queue is wait before the model starts, so it is not kernel time.

problems.title: Wrong rate
problems.promptHtml: A decode measurement says one GPU emits about 210 tokens per second when it is bandwidth-bound at batch 1. Someone forecasts a 1,024-token prefill as 1,024 / 210 seconds. Why is that forecast the wrong shape, and which stage is the 210?
problems.answer: prefill does many tokens of math per weight load, so it is not the decode rate; 210 tokens/s is batch-1 decode.

problems.title: Quiet GPU
problems.promptHtml: A GPU costs $2 per hour and can decode 200 tokens per second when busy. Tonight it averages 20 tokens per second. Compute dollars per million tokens in both cases. What changed, the price of the GPU or the utilization?
problems.answer: busy is about $2.78 per million tokens; quiet is about $27.80 per million; the GPU price stayed $2 and utilization fell.

problems.title: One latency
problems.promptHtml: Short prompts show time to first token of 90 ms and 28 ms between tokens. Long prompts show 640 ms and 31 ms. A chart of "average latency" moved because the product shipped a feature with longer prompts. Which stage moved, and why is a decode-kernel change the wrong first edit?
problems.answer: prefill / time to first token moved with prompt length; inter-token time stayed near 30 ms, so decode was not the regression.

problems.title: Who left
problems.promptHtml: The client gives up at 1,000 ms. The server's clock for a 50-token answer is 200 ms to the first token plus 49 × 40 ms. Will the client still be there for the last token, and what should you log to see that?
problems.answer: no, the server needs about 2,160 ms; log arrived, first token, and last token, and watch client disconnects.

problems.title: Two products
problems.promptHtml: Product A sends 2,000-token prompts and asks for 16 tokens back. Product B sends 32-token prompts and asks for 512 tokens back. They share a replica and a single p95. Which product is buying prefill, which is buying decode, and what split would you put on the dashboard before you buy a second GPU?
problems.answer: A is prefill / time to first token; B is decode / inter-token time; split p95 by stage and by those two shapes.

problems.title: Five times
problems.promptHtml: Serving disks fill and the process never binds a port. The copied directory is 70 GB for a model whose BF16 weights are 14 GB. How many times too large is the copy, what is the extra 56 GB, and what command proves the right artifact before you open the engine version?
problems.answer: 70 / 14 = 5 times; the extra is optimizer state; a dry-load of the exported digest.

bonus.title: Name the stage
bonus.promptHtml: One GPU shows a 4.7 ms lower bound to read 14 GB of weights at 3,000 GB/s. A 1,024-token prefill finishes in 80 ms. A caller with a long prompt complains that the first token is late, and a caller with a short prompt complains that the stream crawls. Which caller is living near the 4.7 ms bound, and which measurement would you refuse to average together?
bonus.answer: the short-prompt decode caller is near the bandwidth bound; refuse to average time to first token with inter-token time.

articles.title: The runtime
articles.html:
The runtime is the process that runs the model: kernels, the cache, the batching loop, and the scheduler inside one replica. When this layer is the problem, the GPU is busy or out of memory and the request never left the machine. You can reproduce it with one replica and a fixed set of prompts.

People point at the runtime first because it is the most visible binary. A lot of pages are not inside it. A runtime profile is the right tool after you know the time is spent on the GPU or in the engine, and the wrong tool when the request is still waiting for a machine, a route, or a deploy.

Mechanism. The runtime loads weights, reserves the cache, builds a batch from the queue, and launches kernels for prefill or decode. It decides which sequences step forward this iteration. It also decides when a sequence is finished and its cache may be freed. Those decisions change latency without any change to the math of attention. A slower kernel and a worse schedule can look the same on a client chart. They do not look the same in a trace that separates queue time inside the engine from kernel time.

Worked numbers. A replica spends 4.7 ms of a decode step moving 14 GB of weights. A schedule that waits 20 ms to fill a bigger batch adds 20 ms before that 4.7 ms starts. The kernel did not get slower. The caller lost 20 / 4.7 ≈ 4 times as much time to the wait as to the memory read. If your profile only shows the kernel, you will tune the 4.7 ms and leave the 20 ms in place.

What fails.

  • A kernel change is proposed while engine queue time is the bar that grew.
  • Cache reservation is sized for the average prompt, then a long prompt is rejected.
  • One replica is profiled under a batch size the balancer never sends.
  • The runtime version changes in the same hour as a traffic shift, and nobody writes down which one moved first.

What you do. On a runtime page, record kernel time and engine queue time separately, plus the batch size and the sequence length. Change the schedule only when the queue inside the engine moved. Change the kernel only when the kernel moved.

engine_queue_ms: 20
kernel_ms: 4.7
batch: 8
max_seq: 8192

articles.title: The infrastructure
articles.html:
Infrastructure is everything that has to be true before the runtime can run: machines, GPUs, the network, the image, the autoscaler, and the load balancer. A perfect kernel still sits idle if no replica is scheduled, or if the balancer keeps sending traffic to a replica that is dead.

This layer fails in whole machines. A node loses a GPU. A deploy rolls an image that cannot allocate the device. A scaler adds replicas that never become ready, so the queue grows while the GPU count on the dashboard goes up. None of that is a change to attention.

Mechanism. A replica is a pod or a process on a machine with a specific GPU. Readiness means the process has loaded weights and is willing to take traffic. The balancer should only send calls to ready replicas. Autoscaling should add replicas when the queue or the latency says you are short, and it should stop adding them when new replicas cannot become ready. A scale-up that ignores readiness just multiplies a broken boot.

Worked numbers. You have 4 ready replicas. Each can start 10 requests per second inside the latency budget, so the fleet can start 40 per second. Traffic arrives at 60 per second. You are short by 60 / 10 − 4 = 2 replicas if the new ones boot cleanly. If a bad image makes every new replica fail readiness, the 5th and 6th pods sit there and you are still short by 2. The pod count went from 4 to 6. Capacity stayed 40 per second.

What fails.

  • The scaler counts pods, not ready pods.
  • Traffic keeps flowing to a replica that failed its health check.
  • A GPU disappears from the machine and the process keeps the same command line.
  • A regional network fault is investigated as a kernel regression because the client latency moved.

What you do. Page on ready replicas and queue depth, not on desired replicas. When capacity is short, compute arrivals divided by the per-replica rate and compare that to the ready count. Roll back the image if new pods do not become ready.

ready: 4
desired: 6
arrivals_per_s: 60
per_replica_rps: 10

articles.title: The tooling
articles.html:
Tooling is how you see and change the other two layers: benchmarks, traces, dashboards, evals, and the client library. A tool does not make the model faster by existing. It tells you which number moved, on which layer, under which input. Without that, every incident becomes a debate about the last binary someone shipped.

The dangerous tool is the one that measures a different job from the one you serve. A benchmark with a fixed batch and a fixed length is useful when production has that batch and that length. It is a different experiment when production is a mix of short and long prompts, or when the client times out before the benchmark's last token.

Mechanism. A trace stitches one request across the gateway, the queue, and the runtime. A benchmark holds the inputs still so you can compare two engines. An eval holds the outputs to a score so a faster checkpoint can be rejected for being worse. The client sets timeouts, retries, and how many tokens it is willing to wait for. Those four tools answer four questions: where did the time go, which build is faster, is the answer still good, and did the caller survive.

Worked numbers. A benchmark reports 2,000 tokens per second at batch 32. Production p95 batch size is 2. The benchmark is not a lie. It is a measurement of a batch you do not have. If batch-1 decode is near 210 tokens per second, quoting 2,000 as the fleet's rate overstates capacity by about 2,000 / 210 ≈ 9.5 times for the traffic that actually arrives one at a time. Use the benchmark to compare builds. Use the production batch to buy GPUs.

What fails.

  • A leaderboard number replaces a trace of the slow request.
  • The eval set never runs, so a quantization is shipped on speed alone.
  • The client's timeout is not in the dashboard, so the server looks healthy while callers retry.
  • Two tools disagree and the team averages them.

What you do. Keep a small fixed prompt set for benchmarks, a trace on the slow requests, and an eval that gates a new digest. Write the client's timeout next to the server's latency so a retry storm is visible.

bench_batch: 32
bench_tok_s: 2000
prod_p95_batch: 2
client_timeout_ms: 1000

articles.title: Route the bug to a layer
articles.html:
The first decision on a page is which layer owns it. Runtime owns kernel time, cache, and the engine's own queue. Infrastructure owns machines, readiness, and the balancer. Tooling owns a measurement that does not match the traffic. Pick the layer before you pick the fix. A kernel patch cannot repair a replica that is not ready. A new dashboard cannot repair a kernel that got slower, but it can stop you from shipping the wrong patch.

Write the layer in the first line of the incident note, with the number that moved and the number that did not. The number that did not move is what keeps the other two layers out of the change.

Mechanism. Each layer has a boundary you can check without a theory. If ready replicas fell, you are in infrastructure even if latency is bad. If ready replicas held and kernel time rose on the same batch and length, you are in the runtime. If the benchmark moved and production did not, or the reverse, you are in the measurement until you show the inputs match. Most long incidents are a layer that was never checked, followed by a week inside the wrong binary.

Worked numbers. Ready replicas stay at 8. Per-token kernel time, measured on a fixed 128-token shape, goes from 5 ms to 9 ms. Client p95 on a 100-token answer goes from 400 ms to 800 ms. The kernel delta is 4 ms per token. Over that answer, 4 × 100 = 400 ms, which is the client move. You do not need a new region. You need the kernel or the engine build that landed on those 8 replicas. If instead ready replicas had fallen from 8 to 3, the same client chart would be a capacity page and the kernel would be innocent.

What fails.

  • All three layers are changed in one rollout, so the next page has no control.
  • The incident note names a vendor and not a number.
  • A green benchmark closes a ticket while production p95 is still bad.
  • Infrastructure is scaled up to hide a runtime regression that burns money on every new replica.

What you do. One layer per change. Record the before and after of the number that owns that layer. Leave the other two frozen until that number moves back.

layer: runtime
ready: 8 -> 8
kernel_ms_per_token: 5 -> 9
held: infra, tooling inputs

problems.title: Inside the machine
problems.promptHtml: Engine queue time inside one replica goes from 2 ms to 20 ms. Kernel time stays at 4.7 ms. Ready replicas stay at 8. Which layer owns the page, and which number would a kernel patch be aiming at?
problems.answer: runtime scheduling, not the kernel; the kernel stayed at 4.7 ms while the engine queue grew.

problems.title: Pods are not capacity
problems.promptHtml: Desired replicas go from 4 to 6. Ready stays at 4. Each ready replica handles 10 requests per second and arrivals are 60 per second. How much capacity did the scale-up add, and how many more ready replicas do you still need?
problems.answer: the scale-up added 0 capacity; you need 60 / 10 − 4 = 2 more ready replicas.

problems.title: Nine times
problems.promptHtml: A benchmark reports 2,000 tokens per second at batch 32. Production batch-1 decode is about 210 tokens per second, and the p95 batch is 2. Why is 2,000 the wrong number to buy GPUs with?
problems.answer: production is not batch 32; 2,000 / 210 ≈ 9.5 times the batch-1 rate, so the leaderboard overstates the traffic you have.

problems.title: Match the delta
problems.promptHtml: Ready replicas stay at 8. Per-token kernel time on a fixed decode goes from 5 ms to 9 ms. Over a 100-token answer, how many milliseconds did the kernel add, and why does that point at the runtime rather than a new region?
problems.answer: 4 × 100 = 400 ms added; ready count did not change, so this is the runtime on the machines you already have.

problems.title: Wrong tool
problems.promptHtml: Production p95 time to first token is 700 ms on long prompts. The benchmark, run at batch 32 on 128-token prompts, got faster after an engine bump. Why does the faster benchmark not close the ticket?
problems.answer: the benchmark inputs are a different batch and length from the long-prompt production traffic.

problems.title: Hide the regression
problems.promptHtml: A runtime regression makes each replica 30% slower. The team doubles the replica count and the client chart returns to the old p95. What did you buy back, and what did the page still cost?
problems.answer: you bought the old latency with about twice the GPUs; the runtime regression is still on every replica.

problems.title: Three checks
problems.promptHtml: Client latency doubles in five minutes. Give one check that would put the page in infrastructure, one that would put it in the runtime, and one that would put it in tooling. Use ready replicas, kernel time, and the benchmark inputs in the answer.
problems.answer: ready replicas fell means infrastructure; ready held and kernel time rose on the same shape means runtime; benchmark and production disagree on batch or length means tooling.

problems.title: One layer
problems.promptHtml: In the last hour someone shipped a new engine, a new instance type, and a new dashboard query. p95 moved. Why can you not name the layer yet, and what would you freeze on the next attempt?
problems.answer: three layers moved at once, so the number has no owner; freeze two layers and change one.

bonus.title: Where the 20 ms went
bonus.promptHtml: A decode step needs about 4.7 ms to read 14 GB of weights. The engine waits 20 ms to build a batch before that read starts. A teammate wants a faster kernel. How much of the caller's wait is the batching delay compared with the memory read, and which layer is the wait in?
bonus.answer: the wait is 20 / 4.7 ≈ 4 times the memory read; the wait is runtime scheduling, not the kernel.

articles.title: Name the job
articles.html:
An inference project starts as a sentence a product manager can check. "Summarize a support ticket in under a second" is a job. "Deploy an LLM" is a pile of hardware. The sentence has to name the input, the output, and the moment the caller needs the output. Everything you measure later hangs off that sentence.

If you skip it, the team optimizes a demo. The demo uses short prompts, a patient operator, and a batch size of one on a quiet GPU. Production uses the prompt the feature actually builds, a timeout in the client, and a burst when a cron job starts. Those are different jobs. A model that wins the demo can miss the feature, and a model that looks slow in the demo can be the right one for an overnight batch.

Mechanism. Write the job as four fields: input shape, output shape, deadline, and what happens when you miss the deadline. Input shape is tokens, pixels, or seconds of audio, with a p95 and a max you will refuse. Output shape is how many tokens you will generate, or how many images, and whether the caller streams. The deadline is a percentile, not a hope. The miss policy is a fallback: a smaller model, a cached answer, or an error the product can explain. Without a miss policy, every incident becomes "make it faster" with no floor.

Worked numbers. Support summaries take a p95 prompt of 1,500 tokens and return about 120 tokens. The client times out at 2,000 ms. If time to first token is 400 ms and tokens arrive every 15 ms, the answer costs 400 + 119 × 15 = 400 + 1,785 = 2,185 ms. That misses a 2,000 ms timeout by 185 ms. You can see the miss before you pick an engine. Either the product accepts a 2,500 ms timeout, the summary is capped near 100 tokens, or you need a faster first token. Arguing about CUDA before this arithmetic is how a quarter disappears.

What fails.

  • The ticket says "low latency" and never names a millisecond.
  • The demo prompt is 64 tokens and production p95 is 1,500.
  • There is no max length, so one caller can pin the replica.
  • Missing the deadline has no fallback, so the client retries and doubles the load.

What you do. Put the four fields in the design doc and refuse engine work until they are numbers. Recompute the timeout whenever the prompt template grows.

input_p95_tokens: 1500
output_tokens: 120
client_timeout_ms: 2000
miss: cap output, do not retry the same model

articles.title: Online and offline
articles.html:
Online inference has a person or a request waiting. Offline inference has a pile of work and a time by which the pile must be done. The same model can serve both, and the right machine plan is still different. Online work buys tail latency. Offline work buys tokens per dollar, and it can wait for a full batch.

Mixing them on one replica without a rule means the batch job fills the GPU and the person waits. Splitting them without a reason means you buy two stacks for one checkpoint. The decision is about the deadline, not about the logo on the model.

Mechanism. Online requests join a short queue with a timeout. The scheduler should prefer them, cap their batch wait, and shed load when the queue exceeds the deadline. Offline requests can sit in a durable queue, run at a high batch size, and checkpoint their progress so a preempted worker resumes. Preemption is legal for offline work when an online burst arrives, if the offline job recorded how far it got. It is not legal to preempt an online token stream and hope the caller does not notice.

Worked numbers. An offline job must score 10 million documents overnight, in 8 hours. Each document is one 512-token prefill and a tiny classifier head, and a full GPU finishes 1,000 documents per second at batch 64.

1,000 × 3,600 × 8 = 28,800,000 documents in 8 hours on one GPU.

You need 10,000,000 / 28,800,000 ≈ 0.35 of that GPU, so one GPU is enough if it stays up. The same GPU, shared with online chat that needs p95 under 300 ms, cannot sit at batch 64. The overnight math and the chat math are both true. They describe two queues.

What fails.

  • A batch job and a chat product share a replica with one queue.
  • Offline work is given a chat SLO, so it refuses the batch size that makes it cheap.
  • Online work is given an overnight SLO, so tail latency is never paged.
  • A preempted offline worker starts over and misses the morning.

What you do. Two queues, one checkpoint. Online has a latency page. Offline has a deadline and a resume point. When they share GPUs, online preempts and offline continues from the last finished document.

queue: online   deadline_ms: 300   max_wait_ms: 20
queue: offline  deadline: 08:00    resume: document id

articles.title: Who is waiting
articles.html:
A consumer chat user and a business workflow do not buy the same tail. The consumer is often one person who will leave. The business call is often one step inside a larger job that retries, fans out, and holds a transaction open. The GPU does not know the difference. Your queue and your timeout should.

Scale changes the shape again. A prototype with ten users can run on one GPU and still feel fast, because the queue is empty. The same binary at a thousand concurrent users is a scheduling problem. Specializing the kernel before you have the concurrency is how teams spend a month on a 4.7 ms read while the queue sits at 200 ms.

Mechanism. Concurrency is arrivals times service time. If each request holds a slot for half a second and 100 requests arrive per second, you need about 50 in-flight slots or the queue grows. Consumer traffic is spiky and cares about the worst second. Business traffic may be flatter and cares about a contract: a percentile, an error budget, and a region. Either way, write the concurrency down. A kernel optimization that saves 10% of compute does not create slots if you are short by a factor of two.

Worked numbers. Each request occupies a slot for 0.5 s. Arrivals are 100 per second.

100 × 0.5 = 50 slots in flight.

You have 8 replicas with 4 slots each, which is 32 slots. You are short by 50 − 32 = 18 slots, about 18 / 4 = 4.5 replicas. A kernel that makes each request 10% shorter cuts service time to 0.45 s and demand to 45 slots. You are still short. Buying 5 replicas closes it. The kernel can wait.

What fails.

  • A consumer tail and a batch contract share one SLO.
  • Concurrency is guessed from yesterday's mean.
  • A 10% kernel win is treated as a capacity plan.
  • Retries from a business client are counted as new users, so load doubles when you are already late.

What you do. Compute slots as arrivals times service time, compare to replica slots, and put retries in the arrival number. Specialize the runtime after the slot count is in the right order of magnitude.

arrivals_per_s: 100
service_s: 0.5
slots_needed: 50
slots_have: 32

articles.title: A budget you can miss
articles.html:
A latency budget is a stack of allowances that sum to the client's timeout. Gateway, queue, prefill, and decode each get a piece. When the sum exceeds the timeout, you do not have a tuning problem yet. You have a budget that does not fit. Cost has the same shape. Dollars per million tokens times expected volume is the bill. If that bill is over the product's margin, a faster kernel that burns the same GPU-hours does not save you.

Write both budgets before the first benchmark, using the job from the first lesson. Then a benchmark has something to beat. A number with no budget is a leaderboard.

Mechanism. Split the timeout from the outside in. Subtract network and gateway. What remains is the replica's budget. Split that into queue, time to first token, and generation. Generation allowance is inter-token time times the number of tokens you promised. If the generation allowance is negative, the product asked for more tokens than the timeout can hold, and no GPU fixes the sign. Cost is the mirror. Take the busy-GPU price per million tokens, divide by your expected utilization, and multiply by monthly tokens. Compare to the revenue or the cap the product named.

Worked numbers. The client allows 1,000 ms. Network and gateway take 40 ms. The replica has 960 ms. Time to first token is budgeted at 200 ms. The product wants 80 output tokens. The remaining time is 960 − 200 = 760 ms for 79 gaps between tokens, so the inter-token budget is 760 / 79 ≈ 9.6 ms. A GPU whose decode step is 15 ms at this batch cannot meet the budget by scheduling harder. You need fewer output tokens, a looser timeout, or a decode step under 9.6 ms.

On cost: $2.78 per million tokens at full utilization, 40% utilization, so about 2.78 / 0.40 = $6.95 per million. At 2 billion tokens a month that is 2,000 × $6.95 = $13,900. If the product capped inference at $8,000, you are over before you pick a second technique.

What fails.

  • The budget is "as fast as possible."
  • Generation length is unlimited inside a fixed timeout.
  • Cost uses 100% utilization for a service that is busy 40% of the hour.
  • The team beats a benchmark and misses the only number the client enforces.

What you do. Publish the timeout split and the monthly bill at the utilization you measured. If either one does not fit, change the product shape or the GPU count before you open a profiler.

timeout_ms: 1000
ttft_budget_ms: 200
itl_budget_ms: 9.6
usd_per_mtok_at_40pct: 6.95

problems.title: 185 ms over
problems.promptHtml: A summary allows 2,000 ms. Time to first token is 400 ms and 119 further tokens arrive every 15 ms. Does the job fit, and by how many milliseconds?
problems.answer: no; 400 + 119 × 15 = 2,185 ms, which is 185 ms over the timeout.

problems.title: Overnight
problems.promptHtml: One GPU finishes 1,000 documents per second. The job is 10 million documents in 8 hours. How many documents can that GPU finish in the window, and do you need a second GPU for throughput?
problems.answer: 1,000 × 3,600 × 8 = 28.8 million, which covers 10 million, so one GPU is enough for throughput.

problems.title: Slots
problems.promptHtml: 100 requests arrive per second and each holds a slot for 0.5 s. You have 32 slots. How many slots are you short, and why does a 10% faster kernel still leave you short?
problems.answer: need 50, short 18; 10% faster demand is 45 slots, still above 32.

problems.title: 9.6 ms
problems.promptHtml: After network, gateway, and a 200 ms first-token budget, 760 ms remain for 79 inter-token gaps. What is the inter-token budget, and can a 15 ms decode step meet it?
problems.answer: 760 / 79 ≈ 9.6 ms; a 15 ms step cannot meet that budget.

problems.title: Bill
problems.promptHtml: Full-utilization price is $2.78 per million tokens. Utilization is 40%. Volume is 2 billion tokens a month. The product cap is $8,000. What is the bill, and are you inside the cap?

problems.title: One queue
problems.promptHtml: Chat needs p95 under 300 ms. An offline scoring job wants batch 64 and can wait until 08:00. Why is one shared queue the wrong plan even though both jobs load the same checkpoint?
problems.answer: chat is buying tail latency and offline is buying tokens per dollar; a full batch makes the person wait.

problems.title: Retries
problems.promptHtml: Arrivals are 100 per second before retries. When p95 exceeds the timeout, the client retries once, so the server sees about 200 per second. Service time is 0.5 s. How many slots do you need once retries start, and why does adding retries make the miss worse?
problems.answer: 200 × 0.5 = 100 slots; retries double demand while you are already over the deadline.

problems.title: Change the sentence
problems.promptHtml: The four fields say 1,500 input tokens, 120 output tokens, a 2,000 ms client timeout, and no fallback. The arithmetic says the answer takes about 2,185 ms. Name two product changes that make the job fit without a new kernel, and say what you would refuse to do first.
problems.answer: raise the timeout or cap the output tokens (and stop blind retries); refuse to start with a kernel profile.

bonus.title: Which budget broke
bonus.promptHtml: The replica budget allows about 9.6 ms between tokens, and the measured decode step is 15 ms. Separately, the monthly bill at 40% utilization is about $13,900 against an $8,000 cap. A teammate proposes a kernel that makes decode 10% faster and uses the same GPU-hours. Which budget can that kernel touch, and which budget does it leave broken?
bonus.answer: 15 × 0.9 = 13.5 ms, still above 9.6 ms, so latency stays broken; cost stays broken because GPU-hours did not change.

articles.title: Model selection
articles.html:
You pick a model for a job, not for a leaderboard. The inputs that matter are whether it can do the task, whether it fits the memory you have, and whether its latency at your prompt length fits the budget from the previous topic. A larger model can be the wrong answer when a smaller one already clears the quality bar inside the timeout.

Selection is a short list, not a bake-off of everything published this month. Start with the models your serving stack can load. Throw out any that cannot fit, weights plus a realistic cache, on the GPU you will actually rent. Then compare quality on your prompts. Speed is the third filter. A model you cannot serve is not a candidate, no matter how it scores on someone else's set.

Mechanism. Fit is weights plus cache plus a little activation scratch, compared with GPU memory. Quality is a score on a set you froze before you saw the outputs. Latency is time to first token and inter-token time at your p95 length, on the batch you expect. Write the three numbers in a table with one row per candidate. The winner is the cheapest row that clears quality and latency. If none clear both, you do not have a serving problem. You have a job that needs a smaller output, a bigger GPU, or a lower quality bar the product accepts in writing.

Worked numbers. Candidate A is 7B in BF16, 14 GB of weights. Candidate B is 70B in BF16, about 140 GB of weights, so it needs at least two 80 GB GPUs before any cache. Your job's quality bar is 80 on a frozen set of 200 tickets. A scores 84. B scores 86. Both clear 80. A's p95 time to first token on a 1,500-token prompt is 400 ms inside a 2,000 ms budget. B's is 1,800 ms before decode, which already consumes the budget. You ship A. The two extra quality points on B do not fit the timeout, and B costs roughly ten times the weight memory.

What fails.

  • The model is chosen from a chat demo with no frozen eval.
  • A 70B model is selected on a laptop and surprises the GPU order.
  • Quality is re-judged after seeing which model is faster.
  • The table has speed and no memory column.

What you do. Three columns: quality on the frozen set, p95 latency at your length, and bytes to load. Ship the cheapest row that passes the first two. Record the rejected rows so the next person does not rerun the demo.

model: 7B   quality: 84   p95_ttft_ms: 400   weights_gb: 14
model: 70B  quality: 86   p95_ttft_ms: 1800  weights_gb: 140
ship: 7B

articles.title: Quality before speed
articles.html:
A faster wrong answer is a regression. The eval has to be frozen, small enough to run on every candidate, and tied to the product sentence. If the product summarizes tickets, the set is tickets, not a generic exam. If you change the set after the model looks bad, you are grading the model you wish you had.

Speed work comes after a checkpoint clears the bar. Quantization, speculative decoding, and smaller engines can all move quality. The eval is how you notice. A vibe check in a playground will bless a model that fails the tickets you actually have.

Mechanism. Freeze the prompts, the scoring rule, and the pass mark. Run it on the exact digest you will serve, including the tokenizer. A tokenizer mismatch can drop quality with no change to the weights. Store the score next to the digest in the registry. Promotion requires the score at or above the bar. A later speed experiment re-runs the same set. If the score falls through the bar, the experiment does not ship, even if tokens per second doubled.

Worked numbers. The bar is 80 on 200 tickets. The BF16 digest scores 84. An INT8 export scores 83. An INT4 export scores 71. INT8 stays above the bar and halves the weight bytes, from 14 GB to 7 GB. INT4 would cut weights to about 3.5 GB and fails the bar by 80 − 71 = 9 points. You ship INT8. The INT4 speed does not enter production. Re-running the set after you "fix" the prompts to make INT4 pass is a different eval, and it does not count.

What fails.

  • The playground is the eval.
  • The set changes between the BF16 run and the quantized run.
  • The tokenizer in the export differs from the one in the score.
  • A doubled throughput closes the ticket while the score fell from 84 to 71.

What you do. One frozen set, one pass mark, one digest. Attach the score to the artifact. Block promotion when the score is under the bar.

bar: 80
bf16: 84
int8: 83
int4: 71
promote: int8

articles.title: Fine-tuning changes the checkpoint
articles.html:
Fine-tuning is a quality tool. It produces a new checkpoint. It does not change the serving physics by itself. You still have weights, a cache, a latency budget, and an eval. The new file can be larger, it can use a different tokenizer, and it can be worse at the frozen set even when the training loss went down.

Treat the fine-tune as a candidate row in the same table as the base model. If it does not clear the bar, you do not serve it. If it clears the bar and misses latency, you do not relax the timeout quietly. The product either accepts the new deadline or you keep the base model.

Mechanism. A fine-tune reads a base model and a dataset and writes a new digest. Serving should load that digest the same way it loads any other: export to the runtime format, dry-load, score the frozen set, then canary. Training loss is not the frozen set. A canary that looks good on one engineer's prompts is not the frozen set either. Roll forward only when the canary's score and latency both sit inside the budgets. Keep the previous digest pinned so you can roll back without another training run.

Worked numbers. The base model scores 84 and answers inside 2,000 ms. A fine-tune scores 88 on the same 200 tickets and adds 200 ms to time to first token because the prompt template grew by 400 tokens. The timeout is still 2,000 ms. That extra 200 ms pushes the fine-tune past the timeout. The fine-tune is a better answer that does not fit. You either shorten the template, raise the timeout with the product's name on the change, or you keep serving the base digest. Starting a second fine-tune because the first one "feels slow" spends GPUs to avoid that conversation.

What fails.

  • Training loss is used as the promotion gate.
  • The fine-tune is copied to production as trainer shards.
  • The prompt template grows and nobody rechecks the timeout.
  • Rollback needs a retrain because the base digest was deleted.

What you do. Score the fine-tune on the frozen set, time it at the new template length, and pin the previous digest until both gates pass.

base_quality: 84
tune_quality: 88
extra_ttft_ms: 200
decision: template or timeout, base stays pinned

articles.title: Measure latency and throughput
articles.html:
A measurement is a contract about inputs. Latency is a percentile of a clock you named, on a length you named, at a concurrency you named. Throughput is completed work per second under that same contract. Change any of those and you have a new measurement. Comparing them as if they were one number is how a regression hides.

Run the measurement on the artifact you will serve, on a GPU you will rent, with the client timeout turned on. A number taken with timeouts disabled will count tokens the caller will never see.

Mechanism. Fix the prompt set, the output cap, the concurrency, and the clocks. Warm the replica before you record, so the load of the weights is not inside the first request. Record time to first token, inter-token time, and completed requests per second. Also record errors and timeouts as their own rate. A throughput number that counts timed-out requests as successes is a load test of the retry, not of the model. Repeat once. If the two runs disagree by more than the noise you allow, you do not have a result yet.

Worked numbers. Concurrency is 8. Each request generates 100 tokens and the step is 10 ms, so one request takes about 1 s of decode plus a 100 ms prefill, about 1.1 s. Throughput is roughly 8 / 1.1 ≈ 7.3 requests per second, or 7.3 × 100 = 730 tokens per second, if none time out. The client timeout is 1,000 ms. The 1.1 s answer misses it. Completed requests inside the timeout are about 0 per second even though the GPU emitted 730 tokens per second. Report both. Buying GPUs against the 730 figure plans a service the client will not wait for.

What fails.

  • The first request after boot is included in the latency mean.
  • Timeouts are excluded from the error rate.
  • Throughput is tokens generated, including tokens past the client timeout.
  • Two runs a day apart used different prompt lengths and the chart is titled as one metric.

What you do. Write the contract next to the number: percentile, clock, length, concurrency, timeout. Reject a comparison when any of those differ.

concurrency: 8
p95_ttft_ms: 100
p95_e2e_ms: 1100
client_timeout_ms: 1000
goodput_rps: 0

problems.title: Ship the smaller one
problems.promptHtml: A 7B model scores 84 with 400 ms time to first token and 14 GB of weights. A 70B model scores 86 with 1,800 ms and about 140 GB. The quality bar is 80 and the timeout is 2,000 ms before decode is even added. Which row do you ship, and why is the higher score not enough?
problems.answer: ship 7B; both clear 80, and 70B already uses 1,800 ms of a 2,000 ms budget before decode.

problems.title: Nine points under
problems.promptHtml: The bar is 80. BF16 scores 84, INT8 scores 83, INT4 scores 71. Which exports may be promoted, and by how many points does INT4 miss?
problems.answer: BF16 and INT8; INT4 misses by 80 − 71 = 9 points.

problems.title: Loss is not the set
problems.promptHtml: A fine-tune's training loss is lower than the base run. The frozen ticket set has not been scored. What are you missing before you pin the new digest, and why is the loss the wrong gate?
problems.answer: the frozen-set score and a latency check; training loss is not the product eval.

problems.title: Goodput
problems.promptHtml: At concurrency 8, answers take about 1.1 s and the GPU emits about 730 tokens per second. The client timeout is 1,000 ms. What is goodput in requests per second, and why is 730 the wrong capacity number?
problems.answer: goodput is about 0 requests per second inside the timeout; 730 counts tokens the caller will not wait for.

problems.title: Template grew
problems.promptHtml: A fine-tune scores 88 against a base score of 84, and the new template adds 200 ms to time to first token. The base answers inside a 2,000 ms timeout. The extra 200 ms pushes the fine-tune past that timeout. Why does the higher score stay off the pin?
problems.answer: the base fit, and the extra 200 ms pushes the fine-tune over the timeout; quality cleared and latency did not.

problems.title: Tokenizer
problems.promptHtml: The weights hash matches the scored digest. The export swapped the tokenizer. The frozen set has not been rerun. Why is the score you have not a score for the artifact you are about to serve?
problems.answer: tokenization changed the inputs the model sees, so the old score does not apply to this bundle.

problems.title: Third filter
problems.promptHtml: Four candidates all score above the quality bar. One does not fit on the GPU you can rent. One fits and misses the latency budget. Two fit and meet latency: one costs $6 per million tokens and the other costs $4. State the order of the filters and which candidate is left.
problems.answer: fit, then quality, then latency, and among rows that pass you take the cheapest; the $4 row is the one you ship.

problems.title: Two runs
problems.promptHtml: Monday's benchmark used 128-token prompts at concurrency 1. Thursday's used 1,500-token prompts at concurrency 8. Thursday looks slower. Why can you not call that a regression yet, and which fields must match before you can?
problems.answer: length and concurrency changed, so it is a different contract; match percentile, clock, length, concurrency, and timeout.

bonus.title: The row you reject
bonus.promptHtml: Your table has a 7B model at quality 84, 400 ms, 14 GB, and a fine-tune at quality 88 that misses a 2,000 ms timeout. INT4 of the 7B model would be about 3.5 GB and scores 71 against a bar of 80. Which artifacts do you refuse, and which single row is allowed to take traffic?
bonus.answer: refuse the fine-tune on latency and INT4 on quality; the 7B model that scored 84 and fits the budget is the row that serves.

articles.title: The forward pass
articles.html:
A language model is a stack of blocks. Each block reads the hidden state for the tokens in this step, applies attention and a feed-forward network, and writes a new hidden state. Prefill runs that stack over the whole prompt. Decode runs it once per new token. The weights inside the block do not change between those calls. The cache does.

You do not need to derive attention from scratch to serve the model. You do need to know which tensors are large, because those tensors are the bytes you move and the bytes you store. The large ones are the weight matrices in each block and the cache of keys and values.

Mechanism. One decode step loads the weights for every block, reads the cache for the tokens already produced, computes one new token's queries, keys, and values, appends the new key and value to the cache, and projects a distribution over the vocabulary. Sampling picks the next id. The id goes back in as the next step's input. Nothing in that loop updates a weight. If the output looks wrong and the digest did not change, look at the tokenizer, the sampling parameters, and the cache, in that order.

Worked numbers. A 7B model has on the order of 32 blocks. A forward pass at decode touches essentially all of the 14 GB of BF16 weights once per token at batch 1. At 3,000 GB/s that read is 14 / 3,000 ≈ 4.7 ms, before you add the cache read. Thirty-two blocks do not mean thirty-two separate trips if the runtime fuses kernels, but the bytes still have to come from memory. A plan that ignores the 14 GB and optimizes a tiny vocabulary kernel is aimed at the small tensor.

What fails.

  • Sampling temperature is tuned to fix a tokenizer bug.
  • A quality drop is blamed on weights that did not change.
  • Someone counts parameters and forgets the cache grows with length.
  • Fusion is expected to remove the weight read. It only removes launches around it.

What you do. On a bad answer, compare the digest and the tokenizer to the scored bundle, then the sampling config, then whether the cache was reused from a different prompt. On a slow step, start with the weight bytes and the cache bytes, not the sampler.

digest: run-1842
temperature: 0
cache: fresh
weights_gb: 14

articles.title: Attention
articles.html:
Attention is how each token looks at the tokens before it. The cost depends on how many tokens are in that lookback and on how the cache is stored. Prefill builds the lookback for the prompt. Decode adds one token and looks back over everything already cached. Long contexts are expensive because the lookback gets long, not because the vocabulary got larger.

Multi-head attention stores a key and a value per head. Grouped-query attention uses fewer key and value heads than query heads, so the cache shrinks. That is a serving fact, not a trivia fact. The same parameter count can hide a very different cache.

Mechanism. For each new token the runtime computes a query and compares it to cached keys. The scores pick a mix of cached values. The cache is append-only for that sequence until the sequence ends or is evicted. Sequences do not share a cache unless you deliberately reuse a common prefix. A bug that reuses a cache across unrelated prompts will look like a fast, wrong answer. A bug that never reuses a shared system prompt will look like a correct, slow answer.

Worked numbers. Full multi-head attention with 32 query heads and 32 key-value heads stores 32 key-value heads. Grouped-query attention with 32 query heads and 8 key-value heads stores 8. The key-value cache is 32 / 8 = 4 times smaller for the same sequence length, head dimension, and bytes per element. A 16,000-token prompt that did not fit can fit after that change, or the same GPU can hold more concurrent sequences. You pay whatever quality the model card already measured. You do not get to invent the quality delta at serving time.

What fails.

  • Context length is raised until the cache allocation fails, and the failure is called a kernel bug.
  • A shared system prompt is recomputed for every user.
  • A cache from user A is applied to user B and the answer leaks or drifts.
  • Head counts are ignored, so two "7B" models are planned with the same cache budget.

What you do. Read the number of key-value heads from the config before you size memory. Isolate caches per sequence. Reuse a prefix only when the token ids match from the start of the sequence.

num_attention_heads: 32
num_key_value_heads: 8
kv_shrink: 4x versus multi-head

articles.title: The KV cache
articles.html:
The KV cache is the serving state. Weights are shared by every request on the replica. The cache is not. It grows with the number of sequences in flight and with their lengths. Running out of memory during serving is usually a cache problem, or a reservation problem, once the weights have been shown to fit.

Engines reserve cache in blocks so they can pack sequences without allocating one giant contiguous span per request. The reservation still has to be honest. If you allow 8,000 tokens and 32 sequences, the allocator must be able to hold that, or it must refuse work before the kernel crashes.

Mechanism. For each layer, each key-value head, and each token, the cache stores a key vector and a value vector. Bytes are layers × key-value heads × head dimension × tokens × 2 (key and value) × bytes per element. The runtime asks for a block when a sequence grows and returns blocks when the sequence finishes. Eviction drops a sequence's blocks. A prefix cache keeps blocks whose token ids match a shared prefix so the next request can skip that prefill. Evicting the wrong blocks forces that prefill to run again.

Worked numbers. 32 layers, 8 key-value heads, head dimension 128, BF16 so 2 bytes, one sequence of 2,048 tokens.

Bytes = 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2,048 × 2.

2 × 32 = 64. 64 × 8 = 512. 512 × 128 = 65,536. 65,536 × 2,048 = 134,217,728. Times 2 bytes = 268,435,456 bytes ≈ 256 MB.

Weights are 14 GB. One such sequence is a small addition. Thirty-two of them are 32 × 0.256 ≈ 8.2 GB. At 8,192 tokens the cache is four times larger, about 1 GB per sequence, and 32 sequences are about 32 GB. An 80 GB GPU that looked empty next to 14 GB of weights is now tight. Size the long case, not the average case.

What fails.

  • Memory is planned as weights only.
  • Max sequence length is raised in config without recomputing the cache.
  • A leak keeps blocks after the request finishes, so concurrency slowly dies.
  • Prefix cache hits are assumed for prompts that differ in the first tokens.

What you do. Compute cache bytes at max length times max sequences. Alert on allocation failures and on blocks that do not return after a request ends.

layers: 32
kv_heads: 8
seq: 2048
cache_mb: 256

articles.title: Mixture of experts
articles.html:
A mixture-of-experts block does not run every parameter for every token. A router picks a few experts, and only those experts' weights are used for that token. The file on disk can be much larger than the weights you touch for one token. Serving still has to decide whether the unused experts stay in GPU memory.

If all experts stay resident, memory looks like a dense model of the full size. If experts are swapped from host memory, you trade memory for a stall while the next expert loads. That stall can erase the benefit of skipping arithmetic. The router also has to be deterministic enough that a quality eval matches production. A router that depends on batch composition can make the same prompt take a different expert path in a batch of one and a batch of thirty-two.

Mechanism. Each token produces router scores. The top experts run their feed-forward weights. The others stay idle for that token. Different tokens in the same batch can select different experts, so a batch does not become a single matrix multiply over one expert. The runtime either gathers token slices per expert or accepts idle experts in the batch. Both choices change kernel efficiency. Capacity limits drop tokens to a backup expert when an expert is oversubscribed. Those drops change quality under load even though the checkpoint did not change.

Worked numbers. A model file is 140 GB. Suppose 40 GB is shared attention and the router, and 100 GB is the experts, 8 of them, with the router keeping 2. A dense read of the whole file at 3,000 GB/s would take 140 / 3,000 ≈ 47 ms. The shared 40 GB is read on every token: 40 / 3,000 ≈ 13 ms. Two of eight experts are 100 × 2 / 8 = 25 GB, which is 25 / 3,000 ≈ 8 ms. The step is about 13 + 8 = 21 ms. The 2/8 factor applies to the expert block, not to the whole file. If all 140 GB stay in GPU memory, you pay the memory, not the 47 ms, on every step. If an expert load from the host takes 20 ms, the swap is slower than the 8 ms of expert traffic you hoped to skip. Measure the path you actually configured.

What fails.

  • Disk size is treated as bytes read per token.
  • Expert swaps are enabled and latency grows under a diverse batch.
  • An expert capacity limit silently drops tokens and quality falls only at peak.
  • The eval runs at batch 1 and production runs at batch 32, so the router sees a different mix.

What you do. Record resident expert bytes, whether swapping is on, and the capacity-drop counter. Evaluate at a batch size close to production. Turn swapping off when the host load is slower than the experts you wanted to skip.

experts: 8
active: 2
resident: all
swap_ms: 20
capacity_drops: 0

problems.title: Weights stay put
problems.promptHtml: Answers get worse over an hour. The digest hash is unchanged. Sampling is still temperature 0. Name two places you look before you retrain, and say what the forward pass is not updating.
problems.answer: tokenizer and cache reuse (or sampling only if it changed); the forward pass does not update weights.

problems.title: Four times
problems.promptHtml: One config has 32 key-value heads. Another has 8, with the same query heads and head dimension. By what factor is the KV cache smaller in the second model, for the same sequence length?
problems.answer: 32 / 8 = 4 times smaller.

problems.title: 256 MB
problems.promptHtml: Cache bytes are 2 × 32 layers × 8 key-value heads × 128 × 2,048 tokens × 2 bytes. About how many megabytes is one sequence, and why is that not the number you plan the GPU against by itself?
problems.answer: about 256 MB; plan max sequences times max length, not one short sequence.

problems.title: Thirty-two sequences
problems.promptHtml: One 2,048-token sequence is about 256 MB of cache. You allow 32 concurrent sequences at 8,192 tokens. About how many gigabytes of cache is that, on top of 14 GB of weights?
problems.answer: 8,192 is 4 × 2,048, so about 1 GB per sequence; 32 GB of cache plus 14 GB of weights.

problems.title: Swap versus skip
problems.promptHtml: Two of eight experts are about 8 ms of expert traffic. Shared weights still take about 13 ms on every token. Loading a swapped expert from the host takes 20 ms. Why can the swap be slower than using the resident experts?
problems.answer: 20 ms of loading is more than the 8 ms of expert traffic you hoped to skip; the shared weights are read either way.

problems.title: Drops at peak
problems.promptHtml: Quality matches the eval all morning and falls at peak. The digest is unchanged. Expert capacity drops climb from 0 to a few percent of tokens. Why is this a serving configuration problem?
problems.answer: overloaded experts are dropping tokens to a backup path; the checkpoint did not change, the batch mix did.

problems.title: Prefix
problems.promptHtml: Every request starts with the same 2,000-token system prompt, then a short user message. A bug reuses the cache only when the entire prompt matches, so the system prompt never hits. Another bug reuses a cache when only the length matches, including across users. What should a correct prefix cache require, and which bug leaks?
problems.answer: token ids must match from the start of the sequence; the length-only reuse leaks or corrupts across users.

problems.title: Small tensor
problems.promptHtml: A profile says the sampler is 0.2 ms and the weight read is about 4.7 ms. A teammate spends the week on the sampler. How many times larger is the weight read, and what does fusion not remove?
problems.answer: 4.7 / 0.2 ≈ 23 times; fusion removes kernel launches, not the need to move the weight bytes.

bonus.title: Size the long case
bonus.promptHtml: Weights are 14 GB on an 80 GB GPU. One 2,048-token sequence is about 256 MB of cache. Someone sets max sequences to 32 and max length to 8,192 because the average prompt is short. Estimate the cache reservation and say why the average prompt is the wrong input to that setting.
bonus.answer: about 32 GB of cache reserved; the allocator has to survive the max, not the average.

articles.title: Arithmetic intensity
articles.html:
A step is compute-bound when the GPU is busy doing math and memory is keeping up. It is memory-bound when the GPU is waiting on bytes. You tell them apart with arithmetic intensity: math operations divided by bytes moved. High intensity can use the chip's peak FLOPs. Low intensity cannot, no matter how large the peak FLOPs number is on the spec sheet.

Decode at batch 1 is the usual low-intensity case. You load a big matrix to produce a small output. Prefill of a long prompt is the usual high-intensity case. The same weights are reused across many tokens of math. A technique that helps one of these can do nothing for the other.

Mechanism. Roofline thinking is enough. The chip has a peak math rate and a peak bandwidth. The intensity of the kernel picks which peak you can hit. If the kernel needs more bytes than the bandwidth can supply in the time the math would have taken, you are memory-bound. Adding FLOPs to the spec sheet does not move that kernel. Raising the batch size can, because one load of the weights is amortized over more tokens. That is why a decode benchmark at batch 1 and a decode benchmark at batch 32 are different bounds.

Worked numbers. A decode step at batch 1 moves about 14 GB of weights and does the math for one token. Intensity is low. The bandwidth bound is about 4.7 ms, as before. Suppose the math itself, at a peak of 1,000 trillion operations per second, would finish in 0.5 ms for that single token. The step takes about 4.7 ms, not 0.5 ms. You are waiting on memory for 4.7 − 0.5 = 4.2 ms. A GPU with twice the FLOPs and the same bandwidth still takes about 4.7 ms. A GPU with twice the bandwidth and the same FLOPs takes about 2.3 ms.

What fails.

  • A higher-FLOP GPU is bought for a bandwidth-bound decode.
  • Batch-1 latency is used to predict a well-batched offline job.
  • A kernel is called slow when it is already at the bandwidth ceiling.
  • Intensity is discussed with no byte count and no operation count.

What you do. For the slow kernel, write bytes moved and a lower bound from bandwidth, and compare it to the time you measured. If they match, stop looking for FLOPs.

bytes_gb: 14
bandwidth_gb_s: 3000
bound_ms: 4.7
measured_ms: 5.1

articles.title: Prefill math and decode bytes
articles.html:
Put the two stages on one request so the split stays concrete. Prefill pays a large compute cost once. Decode pays a bandwidth cost on every token after that. The crossover depends on prompt length and answer length. A chat product with long answers lives in decode. A classification product with a long document and one label lives in prefill.

Capacity planning that uses one tokens-per-second number will buy the wrong thing for one of these products. Split the forecast.

Mechanism. During prefill, tokens of the prompt are known up front, so the implementation can run wide matrix multiplies. During decode, the next token depends on the previous sample, so the steps are serial for that sequence. Batching stacks independent sequences so the serial chains run side by side and share the weight load. It does not make one sequence's token N depend on less than token N − 1. A single long generation stays latency-bound by the decode step even when the replica's aggregate tokens per second look high.

Worked numbers. Prefill of 1,024 tokens takes 80 ms. Decode is 5 ms per token at this batch. A 20-token answer costs 80 + 19 × 5 = 80 + 95 = 175 ms, and prefill is 80 / 175 ≈ 46% of it. A 200-token answer costs 80 + 199 × 5 = 80 + 995 = 1,075 ms, and prefill is 80 / 1,075 ≈ 7% of it. The same model, the same GPU, a different product. Optimizing prefill by 50% saves 40 ms in both cases. On the short answer that is a large slice. On the long answer it is noise next to the 995 ms of decode.

What fails.

  • One optimization is rolled out to every product because the model card is shared.
  • A 50% prefill win is advertised as a 50% end-to-end win on long answers.
  • Classification traffic is planned with a chat decode rate.
  • Serial dependence inside one answer is "fixed" by raising batch size, which helps other sequences and not this answer's next token.

What you do. Forecast each product as prefill time plus decode step times the output length. Spend the week on the term that dominates that sum.

prefill_ms: 80
decode_ms: 5
short_e2e_ms: 175
long_e2e_ms: 1075

articles.title: Image generation
articles.html:
Image generation is usually a loop of many denoising steps, not a token stream. Each step runs the model once. The caller often waits for the last step before they see a picture, unless you deliberately stream previews. There is no time-to-first-token in the chat sense. There is time to the finished image, and it scales with the step count.

The memory shape is different too. You store activations for the latent image at the resolution you chose. A larger resolution can blow memory even when the weight file looked fine for a small preview. Batching is a batch of images, and they should share a size or the pack gets awkward.

Mechanism. Start from noise in a latent tensor. Each step predicts an update and produces a slightly cleaner latent. After a fixed or adaptive number of steps, a decoder turns the latent into pixels. The weights of the denoiser are loaded for every step. Cutting the step count from 30 to 15 nearly cuts the model time in half if each step costs the same, and it can cost quality. Resolution changes the latent bytes and the math. A serving config copied from a 512-pixel preview will not describe a 1024-pixel job.

Worked numbers. One step takes 40 ms. A 30-step image takes 30 × 40 = 1,200 ms of model time, plus 50 ms to decode pixels, 1,250 ms. Cutting to 20 steps saves 10 × 40 = 400 ms and lands at 850 ms, if quality still passes the frozen image eval. Doubling resolution might take a step from 40 ms to 120 ms. Thirty steps then cost 3,600 ms before the pixel decode. The step count and the resolution are the two knobs. A chat-style KV cache setting does not belong on this service.

What fails.

  • A chat timeout and a chat cache config are pasted onto an image route.
  • Step count is cut and no image eval is run.
  • Resolution doubles and the replica OOMs on the latent, which is blamed on the weight file.
  • Throughput is quoted in tokens per second for a model that emits pixels.

What you do. Budget time as steps times time per step, plus the decoder. Gate step-count cuts on a frozen visual eval. Size memory at the largest resolution you allow.

step_ms: 40
steps: 30
model_ms: 1200
decoder_ms: 50

articles.title: Compute the bottleneck
articles.html:
When a request is slow, compute the bound before you read a paper. Identify the stage. Estimate bytes or steps. Compare the estimate to the measurement. If they are close, you are at a ceiling and the next win is a different algorithm, a smaller model, or fewer steps. If the measurement is far above the bound, something else is on the critical path: a queue, a copy, a CPU preprocess, a swap.

This is the whole model chapter in one habit. Language models give you prefill versus decode. Image models give you step count and resolution. The arithmetic is short. The mistake is skipping it.

Mechanism. Write the candidate ceiling in one line. For decode, bytes of weights divided by bandwidth. For prefill, compare measured time with a FLOP estimate if you have one, and at least refuse to use the decode rate. For images, steps times measured step time. Then write the measured time next to it. A ratio near 1 means stop tuning the kernel and change the problem size. A ratio of 5 means the kernel is not your ceiling yet. Look at stalls around it.

Worked numbers. Decode ceiling is 4.7 ms and the step measures 5.1 ms. The ratio is 5.1 / 4.7 ≈ 1.1. You are about 10% off the bandwidth ceiling. A heroic kernel will not give you a 2× decode. A 4.7 ms ceiling that measures 25 ms is a ratio of 25 / 4.7 ≈ 5.3. That 20 ms gap is a stall: a batch wait, a host sync, an expert swap. Profile the gap, not the matmul that already matches the ceiling.

For the image job, 30 × 40 ms = 1,200 ms and the trace says 1,250 ms including the decoder. The model loop is the product. Cutting steps is the lever. Buying FLOPs is a later conversation.

What fails.

  • A paper is implemented while the step is already at the bandwidth ceiling.
  • A 5× gap above the ceiling is "solved" with a new GPU of the same bandwidth.
  • Image time is optimized as if it were a KV cache miss.
  • The ceiling uses a batch size the trace does not have.

What you do. Put the ceiling and the measurement in the ticket. Work the gap when it is large. Change the problem size when the ratio is near one.

decode_ceiling_ms: 4.7
decode_measured_ms: 5.1
ratio: 1.1
decision: not a kernel week

problems.title: Same bandwidth
problems.promptHtml: A decode step is limited by reading 14 GB at 3,000 GB/s, about 4.7 ms. The math would finish in 0.5 ms. Why does a GPU with twice the FLOPs and the same bandwidth stay near 4.7 ms?
problems.answer: the step is memory-bound; extra FLOPs do not move a bandwidth ceiling.

problems.title: Forty milliseconds
problems.promptHtml: Prefill is 80 ms and decode is 5 ms per token. How much end-to-end time does a 50% faster prefill save on a 200-token answer, and why is that a small slice?
problems.answer: it saves 40 ms; the answer is about 1,075 ms, so prefill is about 7% of it.

problems.title: Step count
problems.promptHtml: An image step is 40 ms and you run 30 steps plus a 50 ms decoder. What is the model time, and how many milliseconds do you save by cutting 10 steps if each step stays 40 ms?
problems.answer: 1,200 ms of model time; 10 × 40 = 400 ms saved.

problems.title: Ratio
problems.promptHtml: The bandwidth ceiling is 4.7 ms and the measured decode step is 25 ms. What is the ratio, and do you spend the week on the matmul or on the stall around it?
problems.answer: 25 / 4.7 ≈ 5.3; spend the week on the stall, the matmul is not the ceiling.

problems.title: Resolution
problems.promptHtml: At the preview resolution a step is 40 ms. At double resolution a step is 120 ms, still 30 steps. How long is the model loop, and why is a KV-cache setting the wrong knob?
problems.answer: 30 × 120 = 3,600 ms; image models spend time on denoising steps, not a token cache.

problems.title: Serial token
problems.promptHtml: One user wants a long answer. The replica's aggregate rate is high because other sequences fill the batch. Why can that user's next token still be waiting on a serial decode step?
problems.answer: token N of one sequence depends on token N − 1; batching shares weight loads across sequences and does not remove that dependence.

problems.title: Two products
problems.promptHtml: Product A is a 1,024-token document and a one-token label. Product B is a short prompt and a 200-token answer. Prefill is 80 ms and decode is 5 ms. Which product is mostly prefill, which is mostly decode, and where would you spend a week for B?
problems.answer: A is prefill (one decode step); B is about 995 ms of decode versus 80 ms of prefill, so spend the week on decode.

problems.title: Near the ceiling
problems.promptHtml: Measured decode is 5.1 ms against a 4.7 ms ceiling. A proposal promises to double decode speed with a kernel rewrite. Why is that promise not available, and what change could still move the ceiling?
problems.answer: the ratio is about 1.1, so you are already near the bandwidth bound; more bandwidth, less weight traffic, or a higher batch changes the ceiling, a kernel rewrite does not double it.

bonus.title: Pick the lever
bonus.promptHtml: You have three measurements. Decode is 5.1 ms against a 4.7 ms ceiling. A long answer is 80 ms of prefill plus 995 ms of decode. An image is 30 steps at 40 ms. For each, name the lever you would pull first: a new FLOP-heavy GPU, fewer decode tokens or less weight traffic, or fewer steps.
bonus.answer: decode is already bandwidth-bound so change weight traffic or tokens, not FLOPs; the long answer is decode; the image lever is fewer steps.

articles.title: Compute
articles.html:
Peak FLOPs are the chip's math ceiling. You only reach it when the kernel has enough arithmetic intensity. Inference decode often does not. Quoting peak FLOPs as "how fast this GPU serves tokens" overstates a bandwidth-bound step and understates nothing about a heavy prefill that really is compute-bound.

Read the precision the peak refers to. A number for 8-bit tensor cores is not a number for BF16, and a BF16 number is not a number for FP32. The model has to be running in that precision, in a kernel that uses those units. A framework default can leave the fast units idle.

Mechanism. The hardware has different units for different precisions. Tensor cores do the dense matrix multiplies that dominate transformers when the shapes are friendly. A kernel with a tiny dimension, or a datatype the unit does not accept, falls back to a slower path. Occupancy and launch overhead matter more when the multiply is small, which is another way decode at batch 1 disappoints a peak-FLOP comparison. The useful question is the achieved FLOPs on your kernel, divided by the peak for that precision.

Worked numbers. Suppose the relevant peak is 1,000 TFLOP/s and your prefill kernel sustains 400 TFLOP/s. Utilization of peak is 400 / 1,000 = 0.40, or 40%. That is a real compute kernel with room to improve. A decode step whose math would take 0.5 ms against a 4.7 ms bandwidth floor is not at 40% of a useful ceiling. Dividing its tiny operation count by peak FLOPs and calling the GPU "5% utilized" mixes a bandwidth stall with a math stall. Report achieved FLOPs only for the kernels that are actually compute-bound.

What fails.

  • A GPU is chosen because its peak FLOP number is larger, for a decode workload.
  • The peak is an FP8 figure and the server is running BF16.
  • Low SM utilization on a bandwidth-bound kernel triggers a compute optimization.
  • A marketing TFLOP number is pasted into a capacity spreadsheet.

What you do. Name the precision, the peak at that precision, and the achieved rate on the kernel you care about. If the kernel is bandwidth-bound, do not use the FLOP peak as the capacity input.

precision: bf16
peak_tflops: 1000
prefill_achieved_tflops: 400
decode_bound: bandwidth

articles.title: Memory capacity
articles.html:
Capacity is how many bytes the GPU can hold. Weights, KV cache, activations, and the runtime's own scratch all live there. If they do not fit, the model does not get slower in a smooth way. It fails to load, or it spills, or it refuses new sequences. Spilling to host memory can look like a sudden latency cliff rather than a gentle slowdown.

Leave headroom. A card that is 95% full will fragment, and a new sequence at max length will fail while the average looks fine. The number you plan against is the maximum reservation, not the mean.

Mechanism. The driver reports memory in use and memory reserved. Frameworks often reserve a pool up front. A steady "used" number with allocation failures means the pool is exhausted or fragmented, not that the kernel leaked in the last minute. Multi-GPU serving splits weights or cache across cards. The capacity that matters is then the slice on the fullest card, not the sum across the node, unless every byte can actually be placed on any card. A 160 GB pair does not help a tensor that still has to sit whole on one 80 GB device.

Worked numbers. An 80 GB GPU holds 14 GB of BF16 weights. You reserved about 32 GB of KV cache for the long case in the model chapter. Activations and scratch take 6 GB in this configuration.

14 + 32 + 6 = 52 GB.

Headroom is 80 − 52 = 28 GB, about 35% free. That is a comfortable single-GPU serve. Move to 70B BF16 weights at about 140 GB and one 80 GB card cannot hold the weights alone, before any cache. You need a second card or a smaller dtype. Adding cache math on top of an impossible weight load does not make the plan more precise.

What fails.

  • Capacity is summed across GPUs for a tensor that is not sharded.
  • The plan uses average cache, then the max length OOMs.
  • Host swap hides the OOM and turns it into a latency incident.
  • A memory leak is declared from one allocation failure at a known max reservation.

What you do. Write weights, max cache, and scratch against the card the largest shard sits on. Refuse the config when that sum exceeds the card. Alert on allocation failures separately from average occupancy.

gpu_gb: 80
weights_gb: 14
max_cache_gb: 32
scratch_gb: 6
fit: yes

articles.title: Memory bandwidth
articles.html:
Bandwidth is how fast bytes move between HBM and the compute units. Decode, and any other low-intensity kernel, lives or dies by this number.
