Two GPUs with similar peak FLOPs and very different bandwidth will not decode at the same speed. Two GPUs with similar bandwidth will decode large dense models at similar speeds even when the FLOP peaks differ.

Use the bandwidth for the dtype and the bus you are actually hitting. A spec-sheet peak is an upper bound. A measured copy will be lower. For a first estimate, dividing weight bytes by the published HBM bandwidth is good enough to see whether you are in the right order of magnitude.

Mechanism. Each decode step streams weights through HBM, plus the slice of KV cache for that token's attention. At long contexts the cache stream grows and can rival the weights. At short contexts the weights dominate. The runtime can overlap some copies with math, but it cannot move more bytes per second than the memory system supplies. That is why the 14 GB / 3,000 GB/s estimate keeps returning. It is a ceiling, not a profiler toy.

Worked numbers. GPU A moves 3,000 GB/s. GPU B moves 8,000 GB/s. A 14 GB weight read takes 14 / 3,000 ≈ 4.7 ms on A and 14 / 8,000 = 1.75 ms on B. If decode is bandwidth-bound at batch 1, B is about 4.7 / 1.75 ≈ 2.7 times faster per token, not "a newer generation" in the abstract. A 70B BF16 model at 140 GB takes 140 / 3,000 ≈ 47 ms on A and 140 / 8,000 = 17.5 ms on B, if it fits. If it does not fit, the bandwidth number is irrelevant until capacity is solved.

What fails.

  • A generation upgrade is assumed to speed decode when the new card's bandwidth is the same.
  • Cache traffic at long context is omitted, so the estimate is only the weights.
  • A host-to-device copy is blamed on HBM bandwidth.
  • The model does not fit, and the bandwidth ratio is still used as the latency plan.

What you do. Estimate step time as bytes streamed divided by HBM bandwidth. Include cache bytes when context is long. Check capacity first.

weights_gb: 14
hbm_gb_s: 3000
step_ms: 4.7

articles.title: The roofline
articles.html:
The roofline is the picture that joins compute and bandwidth. Below a ridge point, you are bandwidth-bound and the slope is the bandwidth. Above it, you are compute-bound and the flat line is peak FLOPs. Your kernel is a point: intensity on the x-axis, achieved performance on the y-axis. If the point sits on the roof, more tuning of that kernel has little to give. If it sits well under the roof, something else is wrong: launches, synchronization, a bad shape, or a fallback precision.

You can use this without a plotting library. Compare measured time with the bandwidth floor and with the compute floor. The larger floor is the roof for that kernel. Measured time near that floor means you are on the roof.

Mechanism. Intensity is FLOPs per byte. The ridge is peak FLOPs divided by peak bandwidth. A kernel whose intensity is under the ridge cannot exceed the bandwidth line. A kernel whose intensity is over the ridge cannot exceed the FLOP line. Serving decisions fall out of that. Raise batch size to raise intensity of a weight-heavy decode, moving the point right, until you hit the compute roof or the latency budget. Cut bytes with quantization to lower the bandwidth floor. Do not do both blindly and then be unable to say which roof you moved.

Worked numbers. Peak is 1,000 TFLOP/s and bandwidth is 3,000 GB/s. The ridge intensity is 1,000 / 3,000 ≈ 0.33 TFLOP per GB, or about 330 FLOPs per byte. A decode that moves 14 GB and does math that would take 0.5 ms has an intensity under that ridge: the bandwidth floor is 4.7 ms, larger than 0.5 ms, so the roof is 4.7 ms. A prefill whose compute floor is 80 ms and whose bandwidth floor is 4.7 ms has the compute roof. The two kernels on the same GPU sit on different sides of the ridge. One optimization plan cannot cover both.

What fails.

  • One "GPU utilization" metric is used for a kernel under the ridge and a kernel over it.
  • Batch size is raised until latency breaks, in an attempt to reach a FLOP roof the product does not need.
  • Quantization is applied to a compute-bound prefill and expected to cut the 80 ms in half. It cuts bytes, which were not the roof.
  • The ridge is computed with an FP8 peak and a BF16 kernel.

What you do. For each hot kernel, write the bandwidth floor, the compute floor, and the measured time. Optimize the floor that matches the measurement. Leave the other one alone.

bandwidth_floor_ms: 4.7
compute_floor_ms: 0.5
roof_ms: 4.7
measured_ms: 5.1

problems.title: Which peak
problems.promptHtml: A prefill kernel sustains 400 TFLOP/s against a 1,000 TFLOP/s peak. What fraction of peak is that? Why is that fraction the wrong score for a decode step sitting on a 4.7 ms bandwidth floor?
problems.answer: 400 / 1,000 = 40% of compute peak; decode is bandwidth-bound, so compute utilization is the wrong ceiling.

problems.title: Fifty-two
problems.promptHtml: An 80 GB GPU holds 14 GB of weights, 32 GB of max KV cache, and 6 GB of scratch. Does the model fit, and how much headroom is left?
problems.answer: 14 + 32 + 6 = 52 GB, so it fits, with 80 − 52 = 28 GB left.

problems.title: Two bandwidths
problems.promptHtml: GPU A is 3,000 GB/s and GPU B is 8,000 GB/s. A bandwidth-bound 14 GB read takes about 4.7 ms on A. How long is the same read on B, and about how many times faster is B?

problems.title: Ridge
problems.promptHtml: Peak is 1,000 TFLOP/s and bandwidth is 3,000 GB/s. A kernel's bandwidth floor is 4.7 ms and its compute floor is 0.5 ms. Which floor is the roof, and which purchase does nothing: more FLOPs or more bandwidth?
problems.answer: the roof is 4.7 ms; more FLOPs do nothing while the bandwidth floor is larger.

problems.title: Does not fit
problems.promptHtml: A 70B BF16 model is about 140 GB of weights. You have one 80 GB GPU. Why is a bandwidth comparison not the latency plan yet?
problems.answer: the weights do not fit on one card; capacity fails before bandwidth matters.

problems.title: Wrong sum
problems.promptHtml: Two 80 GB GPUs are on one node, 160 GB total. A weight tensor of 100 GB is not sharded. Can you place it, and why is 160 GB the wrong capacity number?
problems.answer: no; an unsharded tensor has to fit on one 80 GB card.

problems.title: Quantize the right roof
problems.promptHtml: Prefill's compute floor is 80 ms and its bandwidth floor is 4.7 ms. Decode's bandwidth floor is 4.7 ms and its compute floor is 0.5 ms. Quantization cuts weight bytes in half. Which stage's roof moves, and which stage mostly does not?
problems.answer: decode's bandwidth roof moves; prefill is compute-bound at 80 ms, so cutting bytes is not its roof.

problems.title: Precision
problems.promptHtml: The spec sheet highlights an FP8 peak. The server runs BF16 kernels. A capacity sheet uses the FP8 peak to predict prefill. What is wrong with that prediction, and which peak should the sheet use?
problems.answer: the FP8 peak is a different unit from the BF16 kernels that are running; use the BF16 peak.

bonus.title: Three numbers
bonus.promptHtml: You may change one line on a GPU order: peak FLOPs, HBM capacity, or HBM bandwidth. The workload is batch-1 decode of a 14 GB model that already fits, measuring 5.1 ms against a 4.7 ms bandwidth floor. Which line do you change, and why do the other two not move this step?
bonus.answer: change bandwidth; FLOPs are not the roof, and capacity is already sufficient.

articles.title: Generations are spec sheets
articles.html:
NVIDIA datacenter generations are names for a bundle of capacity, bandwidth, compute, and links. Hopper, Blackwell, and whatever ships next are not strategies. They are rows in a table. You read the row for the SKU you can rent, in the precision you will run, and you ignore the family name once the numbers are written down.

SKUs inside one generation still differ. A card with less memory, or a slower link, can share a generation name with the card in the benchmark blog. Buy the SKU, not the adjective.

Mechanism. For each candidate SKU, record HBM capacity, HBM bandwidth, the peak FLOPs at your dtype, and the GPU-to-GPU link bandwidth. Then run the fit test and the bandwidth floor from the previous topic. The generation is only useful as a heading that helps you find those four numbers. A newer generation with the same bandwidth and a higher FLOP peak does not speed a bandwidth-bound decode. An older generation with more memory can be the one that fits.

Worked numbers. SKU H has 80 GB and 3,000 GB/s. SKU B has 80 GB and 8,000 GB/s. Both fit a 14 GB model with the 32 GB cache plan. Decode floors are 4.7 ms and 1.75 ms. If an hour of SKU B costs twice an hour of SKU H, compare tokens, not cards. Suppose batch-1 decode is the whole job. B is about 2.7 times faster per GPU-hour of wall clock, so a 2× price is still a win per token, about 2.7 / 2 = 1.35 times more tokens per dollar, if utilization matches. If the job is a compute-bound prefill already at 40% of a huge FLOP peak on H, you recompute. The generation headline is not an input to either calculation.

What fails.

  • "Get Blackwell" is the capacity plan.
  • A blog benchmark used a different SKU in the same generation.
  • Price per GPU-hour is compared without tokens per second.
  • A newer card with the same HBM size is expected to solve an OOM.

What you do. A four-number row per SKU, then fit and the relevant floor, then price per token at the utilization you expect.

sku_h_gb: 80
sku_h_gb_s: 3000
sku_b_gb_s: 8000
price_ratio: 2

articles.title: An instance is a machine
articles.html:
You rent an instance, not a loose GPU. The instance includes a CPU, host memory, a disk, a network interface, and a count of GPUs that share a box. A model that fits on the GPU can still miss its deadline because tokenization is stuck on a small CPU, or because the image is paging from a slow disk, or because the network into the box is the bottleneck for a large request body.

GPU count on the instance is also a placement constraint. Eight GPUs in one box can talk over a fast link. Eight GPUs in eight boxes talk over the network. A plan that says "8 GPUs" and does not say "1 box" is incomplete for any sharded model.

Mechanism. The host feeds the device. Tokenization, image decode, and RPC all happen on the CPU before a kernel starts. If that work is serial and slow, the GPU waits. Host memory holds the overflow when you swap experts or stage weights. The disk holds the image and the checkpoint. A cold start reads the checkpoint across the network or from disk into GPU memory. That read is not the HBM bandwidth from the spec sheet. It is a different pipe, and it dominates scale-from-zero.

Worked numbers. A 14 GB checkpoint loads into the GPU at 3 GB/s from the host path you measured. Startup takes 14 / 3 ≈ 4.7 s before the first token, every time a replica boots cold. A request that needed a 200 ms first token cannot be served by a replica that is still in that 4.7 s. Autoscaling from zero to meet a chat burst pays 4.7 s plus model init, which is why a minimum replica count exists. Separately, tokenization of a 100,000-token prompt takes 400 ms on one CPU core. The GPU prefill might be 80 ms. The host is the ceiling. More HBM does not move the 400 ms.

What fails.

  • Cold start is omitted from a scale-from-zero design.
  • Tokenization latency is absent from the trace because the trace starts at the first kernel.
  • Eight GPUs are assumed to share a fast link when they are eight instances.
  • Host memory is too small for a weight stage the GPU plan required.

What you do. Measure cold load time and CPU preprocess time on the instance type you will rent. Keep a warm floor of replicas if cold start exceeds the deadline. Draw GPUs that must share a link inside one instance.

checkpoint_gb: 14
load_gb_s: 3
cold_s: 4.7
tokenize_ms: 400

articles.title: The link between GPUs
articles.html:
When one replica uses more than one GPU, those GPUs have to exchange activations or cache traffic every step. The link between them becomes a new ceiling, next to HBM. A fast GPU with a slow link can wait on the other GPU. A pair of GPUs in different machines can be slower than one GPU that actually fits the model.

Know which pattern you are using. Tensor parallelism splits a layer across GPUs and communicates every layer. Pipeline parallelism splits layers into stages and communicates between stages. They stress the link differently. If the model fits on one GPU, do not pay for a link you do not need.

Mechanism. Each communication is a volume of bytes that must cross the link before the next math can proceed, unless the runtime overlaps them. The floor is those bytes divided by link bandwidth, plus a latency term that matters when the messages are small. Small frequent messages are a tensor-parallel decode problem. Large less frequent messages are a pipeline problem. The instance diagram tells you the bandwidth. A cloud network between nodes is not the same as a NVLink-class connection inside a box.

Worked numbers. A tensor-parallel step exchanges 100 MB per GPU per layer, over 32 layers, so 3,200 MB per step. On a 400 GB/s link, the transfer floor is 3.2 / 400 = 0.008 s = 8 ms, if the exchanges cannot overlap the math. A single GPU decode floor was 4.7 ms. Splitting this model across two GPUs made the step slower if the 8 ms sits on the critical path. The split was only justified if the model did not fit, or if a different parallel plan overlaps the copy. "Use two GPUs so it is faster" is not a plan when one GPU already holds the weights.

What fails.

  • Tensor parallelism is turned on for a model that fits on one card, and latency gets worse.
  • The link bandwidth in the spreadsheet is the in-box link, and the job was scheduled across boxes.
  • Pipeline bubbles are ignored, so two GPUs deliver far less than twice the throughput.
  • A network blip between nodes is investigated as an HBM regression.

What you do. If the model fits, start with one GPU. If it does not, write the bytes exchanged per step and divide by the link you will actually get. Place those GPUs on that link.

exchange_mb: 3200
link_gb_s: 400
link_floor_ms: 8
single_gpu_floor_ms: 4.7

articles.title: Other accelerators
articles.html:
Other vendors' accelerators are the same three limits plus a software question: can your engine run the model on that chip, in the precision you need, with a kernel that hits the roof you calculated? A chip with excellent bandwidth and no mature runtime is a research project, not a capacity plan. A chip your engine already supports is a real row in the SKU table.

Portability has a cost. Custom kernels for one vendor do not move. If you depend on them for the last 20% and then switch vendors, you give that 20% back. Keep the portable path fast enough that a second source is possible, and use custom kernels where the roof is worth it.

Mechanism. Translate the other chip into capacity, bandwidth, compute at your dtype, and link bandwidth. Then ask whether the serving stack has a backend that loads your checkpoint and passes the frozen eval. A correct but slow fallback kernel means the spec sheet is not the performance you will get. Measure the same prompt contract you use everywhere else. A vendor demo at a different batch size is a different contract, as in the measurement lesson.

Worked numbers. Accelerator C has 96 GB of memory and 5,000 GB/s. The 14 GB model fits. The bandwidth floor for a 14 GB read is 14 / 5,000 = 2.8 ms, between GPU A at 4.7 ms and GPU B at 1.75 ms. The engine's backend for C is in preview and the measured step is 20 ms. The ratio to the floor is 20 / 2.8 ≈ 7. You are not on the roof. Buying C for its 2.8 ms floor buys you a 20 ms step until the kernel exists. Stay on the chip whose measured step matches its floor, and revisit C when the ratio is near 1.

What fails.

  • A spec sheet is accepted without a measured step on your engine.
  • A demo uses a different precision and batch from production.
  • Custom kernels make a second vendor a rewrite, and the schedule ignores that.
  • The chip fits the weights and the software cannot load the tokenizer bundle.

What you do. Same fit test, same floor, plus a measured step on the engine you run. Adopt the chip when the measurement is near the floor and the eval passes.

floor_ms: 2.8
measured_ms: 20
ratio: 7
decision: not yet

problems.title: Price per token
problems.promptHtml: SKU B is about 2.7 times faster than SKU H on a bandwidth-bound decode and costs 2 times as much per hour. Are you getting more tokens per dollar on B, and by what factor?
problems.answer: yes; 2.7 / 2 = 1.35 times more tokens per dollar if utilization matches.

problems.title: Cold start
problems.promptHtml: A 14 GB checkpoint loads at 3 GB/s. How many seconds is the load, and why can a scale-from-zero replica not meet a 200 ms first-token budget during that load?
problems.answer: 14 / 3 ≈ 4.7 s; the replica is not ready to serve during the load.

problems.title: Host ceiling
problems.promptHtml: Tokenization takes 400 ms and GPU prefill takes 80 ms. Where is the ceiling, and why does more HBM not move it?
problems.answer: the CPU tokenization is the ceiling; HBM does not speed the host preprocess.

problems.title: Link floor
problems.promptHtml: Tensor parallelism exchanges 3,200 MB per step on a 400 GB/s link. What is the transfer floor in milliseconds, and how does it compare with a 4.7 ms single-GPU decode floor?
problems.answer: 3.2 / 400 = 8 ms, which is slower than the 4.7 ms single-GPU floor if it sits on the critical path.

problems.title: Not the roof
problems.promptHtml: Accelerator C's bandwidth floor is 2.8 ms and the measured step on your engine is 20 ms. What is the ratio, and why do you not buy C for the 2.8 ms number yet?
problems.answer: 20 / 2.8 ≈ 7; the software is far under the roof, so you would buy a 20 ms step.

problems.title: One box
problems.promptHtml: A plan says "8 GPUs" for a model that needs a fast link every layer. The scheduler places them as eight single-GPU instances. Which bandwidth did you lose, and why is the HBM spec not the missing number?
problems.answer: the in-box GPU link; the GPUs now talk over the network, which is a different pipe from HBM.

problems.title: SKU not generation
problems.promptHtml: Two cards share a generation name. One has 80 GB and 3,000 GB/s. The other has 40 GB and 3,000 GB/s. Your weights plus max cache are 52 GB. Which card fails, and why is the generation name not the decision?
problems.answer: the 40 GB card fails the fit; capacity differs inside the generation, so the SKU numbers decide.

problems.title: Fits, so one GPU
problems.promptHtml: The model fits on one GPU with a 4.7 ms decode floor. A teammate turns on tensor parallelism across two GPUs and the step becomes slower. Why is that an expected risk, and what byte count would you demand before splitting?
problems.answer: the link exchange can exceed the single-GPU floor; compute bytes exchanged per step divided by the real link before you split.

bonus.title: Order the limits
bonus.promptHtml: A candidate machine fails the weight fit. Another fits, and the measured step is several times the bandwidth floor because the kernel is missing. A third fits, the measured step matches the bandwidth floor, and the price per token is the one you can defend. Which machine do you rent, and which limit stopped the first two?
bonus.answer: rent the third; the first fails capacity and the second is not on the roof in software.

topics.title: From a kernel to a file

articles.title: What CUDA is for
articles.html:
CUDA is how a kernel runs on an NVIDIA GPU. A kernel is a function that many threads execute over a tensor. The serving win is almost never "write CUDA" in the abstract. It is a kernel that is already on the wrong side of the roofline: too many launches, a dtype that missed the tensor cores, or a copy that breaks the overlap. If the measured step already matches the bandwidth floor, a new kernel will not double it.

Most of the time you consume kernels from a library. You need enough of the model to know when the library is falling back, and enough of the tools to see a launch stream that is mostly idle gaps.

Mechanism. The host enqueues kernels on a stream. The device runs them. A synchronization forces the host to wait and often drains the chance to overlap the next copy. Many small kernels pay launch overhead that a fused kernel pays once. Fusion does not reduce the bytes of a weight read that must happen either way. It reduces the gaps between reads. When a profile shows a few large mem-bound kernels and almost no gaps, you are done at this layer. When it shows thousands of tiny kernels and the GPU idle between them, fusion or a better runtime graph is the work.

Worked numbers. A decode step's weight traffic floor is 4.7 ms. A profile shows the matmul itself at 4.9 ms and 0.4 ms of gaps between launches. The gaps are 0.4 / 5.3 ≈ 8% of the step. Fusing them away saves a fraction of a millisecond, not a new product. A different profile shows 4.9 ms of math spread across kernels that sum to 4.9 ms, plus 15 ms of idle waiting on a host sync. That 15 ms is the bug. Removing the sync is worth more than any microkernel. Read the profile before you open a CUDA file.

What fails.

  • A custom kernel is started while the step is already within 10% of the bandwidth floor.
  • A host sync is left in the hot path and blamed on HBM.
  • A fallback to a slow dtype is invisible because nobody logged the kernel name.
  • Fusion is promised to cut weight bytes. It cuts launches.

What you do. Profile one step. If gaps dominate, remove syncs or fuse. If the large kernels already match the floor, stop. Log the kernel and dtype so a fallback is obvious.

floor_ms: 4.7
matmul_ms: 4.9
gap_ms: 0.4
decision: no custom kernel

articles.title: PyTorch is not the server
articles.html:
PyTorch is a fine way to run a forward pass and a poor way to serve a crowd, unless you add the serving pieces yourself. A Python process that calls the model once per request will underfill the GPU, hold the GIL around tokenization, and keep a KV cache in whatever layout you happened to allocate. You can serve a prototype this way. You should not plan a fleet on it once concurrency shows up in the slot math.

The split is simple. Research code answers "is the forward pass correct?" Serving code answers "how do many sequences share the weights and the cache?" The second question is an engine, even if the engine calls PyTorch kernels underneath.

Mechanism. A naive server loads the model, tokenizes on the request thread, runs one forward, and returns. It does not batch across requests, so decode stays at batch 1. It may reallocate the cache every step. It may copy logits back to the CPU to sample in Python, paying a sync each token. An engine keeps sequences in a scheduler, builds a batch, samples on device when it can, and reuses cache blocks. The same PyTorch matmul can sit under both designs. The latency difference is the schedule, not a different brand of multiply.

Worked numbers. Batch-1 decode is 5 ms per token. Ten independent Python workers on one GPU will not give you 10 × the rate if they serialize on the device. They queue. One engine that batches those ten sequences can approach a shared weight load, so the step might stay near 6 or 7 ms for the whole batch instead of 10 × 5 ms. Throughput becomes about 10 tokens / 7 ms ≈ 1,400 tokens per second instead of 1 / 0.005 = 200. The matmul library did not change. The batch did. If your prototype measures 200 tokens per second per GPU, do not buy five times as many GPUs before you turn on a scheduler.

What fails.

  • A Flask or FastAPI handler calls the model once per request and the GPU stays at batch 1.
  • Logits are copied to the CPU every token.
  • The prototype's tokens per second become the capacity spreadsheet.
  • A rewrite of the model in another framework is proposed before batching is turned on.

What you do. Keep PyTorch for the correct forward pass and for tests. Serve with a scheduler that batches and owns the cache. Compare tokens per second before and after batching on the same GPU.

batch1_tok_s: 200
batched_tok_s: 1400
change: scheduler, same matmul

articles.title: Formats the server can load
articles.html:
The server wants a file it can map into tensors: weights, config, and tokenizer, with a dtype and a shape it agrees with. SafeTensors is a common choice because it maps bytes without executing code. A pickle checkpoint can run arbitrary code on load. A trainer shard directory is a third thing. Export is the step that turns the training output into the file the server maps.

Quantized files are also a format. The kernel has to understand the packing. A file that is "INT4 on disk" and dequantizes into a slow path on load did not buy you the bandwidth cut you planned. The format and the kernel are one decision.

Mechanism. Export reads the trained weights, casts or packs them, writes the serving file, and copies the tokenizer and config that match. A digest of that bundle is what you pin. Loading checks shapes against the config. A mismatch fails the boot, which is what you want. A silent reshape would serve nonsense. Startup time includes reading the file into GPU memory, which is the cold-start path from the hardware chapter, not a kernel issue.

Worked numbers. BF16 weights are 14 GB. An INT8 pack of the same matrices is about 7 GB if the scales are small. The export must record the scale with the packed bytes or the loader cannot reconstruct the values. A 14 GB read at 3 GB/s is about 4.7 s. A 7 GB read is about 2.3 s. You saved cold-start time and HBM, and only if the INT8 kernel exists. If the loader upcasts to BF16 on the GPU, you pay the 7 GB of disk and then occupy 14 GB of HBM again. Check resident bytes after load, not the file size in the registry.

What fails.

  • A pickle file is loaded in a service that accepts untrusted checkpoints.
  • The tokenizer is not in the bundle, so the server boots weights that tokenize differently from the eval.
  • File size shrinks and resident GPU bytes do not.
  • Trainer shards are pointed at by the serving pin.

What you do. Export to a mapped format the engine loads, include tokenizer and config, and record resident GPU bytes after a dry-load. Reject pickle for any artifact you did not just build yourself in a trusted job.

format: safetensors
file_gb: 7
resident_gb: 7
tokenizer: included

articles.title: A serving stack
articles.html:
Name the layers in the binary you run, from the socket to the kernel, so a page has an owner. A gateway terminates clients and enforces auth and limits. A scheduler in the engine admits requests and builds batches. A model runner executes prefill and decode. Kernels do the math. Metrics sit beside all of them. When you add a component, say which of those it replaces. "Add a router" is not a layer until you know whether it routes requests or experts.

Distributed runtimes sit in this stack when one model spans GPUs. They are not a replacement for the scheduler. They move tensors. The scheduler still decides which sequences run.

Mechanism. A request flows gateway to scheduler to runner to kernels, then tokens flow back the same way. Each hop adds a clock you can log. The gateway clock includes queueing in front of the engine. The scheduler clock includes waiting for a batch. The runner clock includes prefill and decode. The kernel clock is the device time. A stack diagram with one box called "inference" cannot be paged. Split the clocks until one of them moved.

Worked numbers. End-to-end p95 is 700 ms. Gateway queue is 40 ms. Engine queue is 20 ms. Prefill is 80 ms. Decode of the p95 answer is 400 ms. The sum of those pieces is 540 ms, so about 160 ms is still unaccounted for: network, tokenization, or a client delay. You do not tune kernels against 700 ms. You find the 160 ms, and you notice decode is the largest named piece. A new gateway does not move the 400 ms. A decode change does not move the 40 ms. The stack only helps if the numbers are attached to the boxes.

What fails.

  • One latency number covers gateway, queue, and kernels.
  • A new component is inserted and no clock is added for it.
  • Distributed runtime time is mixed into kernel time, so a link stall looks like a slow matmul.
  • The diagram is redrawn for every incident instead of being the stable map.

What you do. Keep four clocks: gateway, engine queue, prefill, decode. Page the one that moved. Add a component only when you can say which clock it owns.

gateway_ms: 40
engine_queue_ms: 20
prefill_ms: 80
decode_ms: 400

problems.title: Gaps or floor
problems.promptHtml: The bandwidth floor is 4.7 ms. One profile shows a 4.9 ms matmul and 0.4 ms of gaps. Another shows 15 ms waiting on a host sync. Which profile deserves a CUDA change, and which deserves removing a sync?
problems.answer: the 15 ms sync; the 0.4 ms gaps are a small fraction of a step already near the floor.

problems.title: Same matmul
problems.promptHtml: A Python server at batch 1 gets about 200 tokens per second. An engine that batches the same matmul gets about 1,400. What changed, and why is a new framework not the first explanation?
problems.answer: the scheduler and the batch; the matmul library can be the same.

problems.title: Resident bytes
problems.promptHtml: An INT8 file is 7 GB. After load, the GPU still holds 14 GB for the model. Did you get the HBM savings, and what should you measure instead of the file size?
problems.answer: no; measure resident GPU bytes after load.

problems.title: Unaccounted
problems.promptHtml: Gateway 40 ms, engine queue 20 ms, prefill 80 ms, and decode 400 ms sum to 540 ms. End-to-end p95 is 700 ms. How many milliseconds are still unnamed, and why is a kernel tune against 700 ms the wrong scope?
problems.answer: about 160 ms unnamed; the kernel is not the whole 700 ms.

problems.title: Pickle
problems.promptHtml: A teammate wants the server to load a user-uploaded pickle checkpoint because it is convenient. What can that load do, and which format maps bytes without running code?
problems.answer: a pickle can run arbitrary code; a safetensors-style map does not.

problems.title: Tokenizer in the bundle
problems.promptHtml: Weights match the scored digest. The serving bundle omitted the tokenizer and the server used a default one. Why is a green weight hash not enough to promote?
problems.answer: tokenization can differ, so the scored inputs are not the inputs you will serve.

problems.title: Prototype spreadsheet
problems.promptHtml: The only measurement you have is 200 tokens per second from a one-request Python handler. Traffic needs about 1,000 tokens per second. How many of those handlers' worth of GPUs would you buy if you treated 200 as the ceiling, and why might one batched engine on one GPU be enough?
problems.answer: 1,000 / 200 = 5 GPUs; batching can lift the same GPU toward 1,400 tokens per second, so buy the scheduler before the fifth GPU.

problems.title: Name the clock
problems.promptHtml: Decode is 400 ms of a 700 ms p95. A proposal replaces the gateway. Which clock should move if the proposal is the right one, and which clock tells you it was not?
problems.answer: gateway time should move; if gateway stays near 40 ms and decode stays 400 ms, the proposal missed the large piece.

bonus.title: Stop at the floor
bonus.promptHtml: A profile puts the matmul at 4.9 ms against a 4.7 ms floor, with 0.4 ms of launch gaps. A teammate opens a CUDA rewrite to double throughput. What fraction of the step are the gaps, and why is doubling not available from this rewrite?
bonus.answer: gaps are about 0.4 / 5.3 ≈ 8% of the step; the matmul is already near the bandwidth floor, so a rewrite will not double it.

articles.title: What an engine schedules
articles.html:
An inference engine owns admission, batching, the KV cache, and the loop that calls prefill and decode. vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM are engines in this sense. They differ in schedulers and kernels. They do not differ in the job: keep the GPU on the roof you calculated, for the mix of sequences you actually have.

Picking an engine is a measurement, not a slogan. Run your prompt contract on each candidate and keep the one that meets latency at the lowest cost. Revisit the choice when your shape changes, because a scheduler tuned for long decodes can lose on short prefills.

Mechanism. The scheduler decides which waiting sequences enter this iteration, how much of a prefill to chunk, and which cache blocks stay. Continuous batching adds a new sequence to the decode batch when another finishes, instead of waiting for a whole batch to end together. Chunked prefill breaks a long prompt into pieces so a long prefill does not stall decode for everyone else. Those two features are why an engine beats a loop you wrote in a weekend. They also have knobs. A batch cap that is too high grows tail latency. A chunk that is too small grows overhead.

Worked numbers. Three sequences are decoding. A fourth arrives with a 2,000-token prompt. If prefill runs to completion, decode for the three waits for the whole prefill, say 150 ms. If prefill is chunked into 200-token pieces at about 15 ms each, the scheduler can interleave a decode step between chunks. The three sequences see stalls near 15 ms instead of 150 ms. The long prompt still costs about 150 ms of GPU work, but it does not take it in one slice. The caller's time to first token may rise slightly versus an exclusive GPU. The other callers' inter-token time stays inside the budget. That trade is the engine's job to expose, and yours to pick.

What fails.

  • An engine is chosen from a benchmark with one sequence.
  • Chunked prefill is off, and one long prompt freezes every decode.
  • The batch cap is raised until p95 breaks, in exchange for a throughput trophy.
  • Two engines are compared with different max sequence lengths.

What you do. Enable the scheduler features your mix needs. Measure p95 inter-token time with a long prompt in the background. Keep the batch cap inside the latency budget.

background_prefill_ms: 150
chunk_ms: 15
decode_stall_ms: 15

articles.title: vLLM and SGLang
articles.html:
vLLM popularized paged attention: KV cache in blocks, like virtual memory, so sequences of different lengths pack without reserving a worst-case slab for each one up front. SGLang pushes hard on structured generation and on reusing prefixes in a program of calls, which matters when one user request is several model calls that share a prefix. Both are engines you measure. Neither is a default you adopt without the prompt contract.

Use the feature that matches the waste you measured. If waste is fragmentation, paged cache is the point. If waste is recomputing a shared prefix across a chain of calls, prefix reuse is the point. If you need neither, you might still pick one of them because the kernels are on the roof. Say which reason it was.

Mechanism. Paged attention allocates fixed-size blocks as the sequence grows and frees them when it ends. A sequence of 100 tokens does not hold a reservation for 8,000. Prefix caching hashes a block's tokens and reuses the block when the next request starts with the same ids. A chain of calls that repeats a system prompt and a document can hit that cache. A chain that changes the first token misses. Structured generation constrains the sampler to a grammar so the model emits valid JSON or tool calls. The constraint is a runtime feature. It can add overhead and it can save you a retry when the parse would have failed.

Worked numbers. Without paging, 32 sequences each reserve 8,192 tokens even though the average length is 512. That is the 32 GB reservation from earlier, while the average occupancy is 512 / 8,192 = 1/16 of it, about 2 GB. Paging brings the live cache near the real lengths, so the GPU can admit more sequences before it hits the true max. If you still set a concurrency limit of 32 and a max of 8,192, paging does not reduce the worst-case reservation you promised. It reduces waste when most sequences are short. Measure admitted concurrency before and after, at the same tail latency, or you do not know if it paid.

What fails.

  • Paging is turned on and the max reservation is unchanged, then someone expects a smaller GPU.
  • Prefix cache is credited for a speedup on prompts that differ at token 0.
  • A grammar constraint is added and latency moves, with no before-and-after on the same prompts.
  • The engine is swapped in the same hour as the model digest.

What you do. Change one thing. For paging, report concurrency at a fixed p95. For prefix cache, report hit rate and the fraction of prompt tokens skipped. Leave the digest pinned.

avg_len: 512
max_len: 8192
reserved_without_paging_gb: 32
live_gb: 2

articles.title: TensorRT-LLM and multi-GPU serving
articles.html:
TensorRT-LLM compiles a model into a runtime tuned for NVIDIA GPUs: specific shapes, dtypes, and fusions. The win shows up when your shapes are stable. The cost shows up when they are not. A new sequence length, a new batch cap, or a new GPU can mean a new build. Dynamo and similar systems sit above an engine and route work across many GPUs and many model copies: they are infrastructure plus a scheduler, not a kernel.

Use a compiler when the same shapes run all day and the roofline says the current kernels are leaving the roof. Use a multi-GPU router when one replica is not enough or one GPU cannot hold the model. Do not confuse those tools.

Mechanism. A compiled engine selects kernels for a profile of shapes you declared. Requests inside the profile hit the fast path. Requests outside it fall back or fail. Multi-GPU serving either shards one model or replicas many copies. Sharding needs the link from the hardware chapter. Replicas need a balancer. A system that does both still has to decide, for each request, which copy and which shard. That decision is a queueing problem. A faster kernel on each GPU does not fix a router that piles every request onto one copy.

Worked numbers. Compilation cuts a compute-bound prefill from 80 ms to 50 ms on the profiled shape, a 30 ms win. Your p95 prompt is inside the profile, so you can keep it. A second product sends prompts twice as long, outside the profile, and falls back to a path that takes 120 ms. You did not get a 30 ms win for that product. You got a regression. Build a profile that includes the second length, or send that product to a different engine. On the router: 4 replicas at 10 requests per second is 40. If the router sends 30 per second to one of them, that replica's queue explodes while three sit idle. The kernel was not the bug.

What fails.

  • A compiled engine is shipped without the production shape in the profile.
  • A fallback path is slower than the engine you replaced, and only some prompts hit it.
  • A multi-GPU router imbalance is profiled as a kernel regression.
  • Dynamo, or any router, is expected to make a single short of memory model fit without sharding.

What you do. List the shapes in the build. Measure the fallback. Balance across replicas and shard only when one GPU cannot hold the model or the link math says so.

in_profile_ms: 50
fallback_ms: 120
replica_rps: [30, 4, 3, 3]

articles.title: A benchmark you can trust
articles.html:
A benchmark compares two builds under one contract. The contract is the prompt set, the output cap, the concurrency, the percentile, and the timeout. Change one and you started a new experiment. A number from a vendor, a number from last Tuesday, and a number from production can all be true and still be incomparable.

Warm up, then record. Include errors. Publish the contract in the same sentence as the result. When you tune, move one knob and rerun the same contract. A week of knobs with no frozen contract is a diary, not a result.

Mechanism. The harness sends the fixed set at the fixed concurrency, discards the warmup window, and computes p50 and p95 for time to first token and for inter-token time, plus completed requests per second inside the timeout. It logs the engine version, the digest, the GPU SKU, and the knobs. One knob moves per run. If you cannot say which knob moved, you cannot keep the win. Noise is real: run twice. If p95 moves by less than the gap between your two baselines, you did not win.

Worked numbers. Baseline p95 time to first token is 200 ms and 206 ms on two identical runs. The noise band is about 6 ms. A kernel change measures 190 ms. The improvement is 10 ms against a neighbor baseline of 200, which is larger than 6 ms, so it is a real but small win. A change that measures 198 ms is inside the noise. Shipping it because the chart went down is how you collect risk for free. Throughput moves from 700 to 900 tokens per second at the same concurrency, a clear win, and p95 moves from 200 ms to 280 ms. You do not get to keep the throughput and ignore the percentile the product bought.

What fails.

  • Warmup is included and the first request dominates the mean.
  • Two engines are compared at different concurrency.
  • A 4 ms move is shipped when identical runs already differ by 6 ms.
  • Throughput is improved and the latency budget is quietly dropped.

What you do. Freeze the contract. Run the baseline twice. Accept a win only when it beats the noise and stays inside the latency and quality gates.

baseline_p95_ms: [200, 206]
candidate_p95_ms: 190
noise_ms: 6
keep: latency win, recheck quality

problems.title: Chunk the prefill
problems.promptHtml: A 2,000-token prefill takes 150 ms if it runs straight through. Chunks of about 15 ms can be interleaved with decode. What stall do the other sequences see in each design?
problems.answer: about 150 ms if prefill is exclusive; about 15 ms if a decode step runs between chunks.

problems.title: Average is not the reservation
problems.promptHtml: Average length is 512 tokens and max is 8,192. Without paging, 32 sequences reserve the max. Why can live cache be near 2 GB while the reservation is about 32 GB?
problems.answer: 512 / 8,192 = 1/16, and 32 GB / 16 ≈ 2 GB; the reservation is the max, the live cache is the actual lengths.

problems.title: Outside the profile
problems.promptHtml: In-profile prefill is 50 ms. Prompts outside the compiled profile fall back to 120 ms. The old engine was 80 ms. For the out-of-profile product, did you improve or regress?
problems.answer: regress; 120 ms is slower than the 80 ms engine you replaced.

problems.title: Noise
problems.promptHtml: Two baselines measure 200 ms and 206 ms. A candidate measures 198 ms. Is that a win, and what band did you use?
problems.answer: no; the baselines already differ by about 6 ms, and 198 ms is inside that noise.

problems.title: Imbalance
problems.promptHtml: Four replicas can each take 10 requests per second. The router sends 30, 4, 3, and 3. Why is the queue growing, and why is a kernel profile of the busy replica the second look?
problems.answer: one replica is over its 10 per second while others are idle; fix the router before tuning the kernel.

problems.title: Prefix hit
problems.promptHtml: A prefix cache is enabled. Prompts share a 2,000-token system prompt but the first token differs per tenant because a tenant id was prepended. Why is the hit rate near zero?
problems.answer: a prefix hit requires matching token ids from the start; a different first token misses.

problems.title: Throughput against the budget
problems.promptHtml: A candidate raises throughput from 700 to 900 tokens per second and p95 time to first token from 200 ms to 280 ms. The budget is 220 ms. What do you keep, and what do you reject?
problems.answer: reject the candidate for latency; the throughput win does not clear a 220 ms p95 budget.

problems.title: One knob
problems.promptHtml: Over one afternoon you change the engine, the digest, and the batch cap. p95 improves by 40 ms. Why is that not a result you can keep with confidence, and what would a trustworthy rerun change?
problems.answer: three knobs moved, so the 40 ms has no owner; rerun with one knob against a twice-run baseline.

bonus.title: Feature for the waste
bonus.promptHtml: You measured two kinds of waste. Most sequences are far shorter than the max, so a worst-case reservation leaves the GPU idle. Separately, a chain of calls repeats a long shared prefix and pays prefill every time. Which engine feature matches each waste, and what single number would you report for each?
bonus.answer: paging for the short sequences, report concurrency at a fixed p95; prefix cache for the repeated prefix, report hit rate or tokens skipped.

articles.title: Quantization
articles.html:
Quantization stores weights, and sometimes the cache, in fewer bits. BF16 is 2 bytes per parameter. INT8 is 1 byte. INT4 packed well is about half a byte. The bandwidth floor for a weight-bound decode drops with the bytes you actually stream from HBM. If the kernel upcasts to BF16 before the multiply and the wide values stay resident, you paid for a small file and kept the old floor.

Scales and zeros have to travel with the packed weights. A scheme the kernel does not implement is a file you cannot serve. Pick the scheme your engine already runs, then measure.

Mechanism. Weights are divided into groups. Each group stores a scale and a small integer per element. The kernel multiplies using those integers, or dequantizes into a register and multiplies. Per-channel and per-group scales cost a little extra memory and a little extra math, and they are why quality survives. Activation quantization is a second choice, with its own scales, and it is more sensitive. Start with weights. Touch activations when weight-only quantization is not enough and the eval still passes.

Worked numbers. A 14 GB BF16 model streams in about 4.7 ms at 3,000 GB/s. INT8 weights are about 7 GB, so the floor is 7 / 3,000 ≈ 2.3 ms, roughly half, if the kernel streams 7 GB. INT4 weights are about 3.5 GB, and the floor is 3.5 / 3,000 ≈ 1.2 ms. A measured INT8 step of 2.5 ms is near that roof. A measured INT8 step of 4.6 ms means you are still moving about 14 GB. Check resident traffic, not the brochure. Halving the floor only matters for the bandwidth-bound stage. A compute-bound prefill at 80 ms does not become 40 ms because the file got smaller.

What fails.

  • File size shrinks and the decode step stays at 4.7 ms.
  • INT4 is shipped because the floor math looked good, with no eval.
  • Quantization is expected to cut prefill time in half on a compute-bound model.
  • A scheme is chosen that the production engine cannot run, so every request hits a slow dequant path.

What you do. Record bytes streamed and the step time before and after. Keep the quant only when the step moves toward the new floor and the frozen eval still passes.

bf16_floor_ms: 4.7
int8_floor_ms: 2.3
int8_measured_ms: 2.5
keep: int8

articles.title: Check quality after you quantize
articles.html:
The eval from the prerequisites chapter is the gate. Run it on the quantized digest with the same tokenizer and the same prompts. A small drop can be acceptable if you wrote the bar down first. A drop through the bar is a reject, even if tokens per second doubled. Do not retune the eval to recover a technique.

Some failures are bursty. Averages stay high while a slice of prompts, long contexts or numeric answers, falls apart. Slice the eval the way the product is sliced. A mean of 83 can hide a slice at 60.

Mechanism. Compare the quantized candidate to the BF16 baseline on the frozen set, overall and by slice. Log the largest regressions with the prompt ids. If a slice is the product, that slice is the bar. Calibration data for the quantizer should look like production inputs. Calibrating on a generic corpus and serving tickets is how a scheme that "usually works" misses your job. When you reject a quant, keep the note so the next person does not rerun INT4 on the same model and the same bar.

Worked numbers. The bar is 80. BF16 scores 84 overall, 82 on the numeric slice. INT8 scores 83 overall and 81 on the numeric slice. Both slices stay above 80. INT4 scores 79 overall and 61 on the numeric slice. Overall, INT4 misses by 1 point. On the slice that is the actual product, it misses by 80 − 61 = 19 points. You reject INT4 even if a dashboard that only shows the mean is waved around, and you would still reject it if someone rounds 79 up. INT8 ships. The numeric slice is why you sliced at all.

What fails.

  • Only the overall mean is reported.
  • The bar moves from 80 to 79 after INT4 scores 79.
  • Calibration prompts are nothing like the tickets you serve.
  • The quantized eval uses a different tokenizer "because the exporter swapped it."

What you do. Publish overall and the product slice, for BF16 and for the candidate, against a bar you do not edit in the same change.

bar: 80
int8_overall: 83
int8_numeric: 81
int4_numeric: 61
ship: int8

articles.title: KV cache reuse
articles.html:
Reuse means not recomputing a prefix you have already paid to prefill. The cache blocks for those tokens are kept and matched against the next request. A shared system prompt, a repeated document, or a multi-turn conversation that grows by a few tokens are the cases. The match is on token ids from the start of the sequence. Anything else is a bug.

Reuse saves prefill time. It does not make decode cheaper for the new tokens, except that the cache those new tokens attend to is already there. A product whose time is almost all decode will see a small win. A product whose time is a long repeated prefill will see a large one.

Mechanism. The engine hashes or compares prefix blocks and, on a hit, skips the prefill for those tokens and starts from the first new token. The blocks must stay in GPU memory, or the hit becomes a reload. Eviction policy decides which prefixes survive. A huge unique prefix per user will not hit and will crowd out the shared one. Admission should prefer keeping the prefix that many requests share. Hits are a rate you can plot. A feature with a near-zero hit rate is not a speedup, no matter how elegant the hashing is.

Worked numbers. A 2,000-token system prompt takes 150 ms to prefill. The user message adds 100 tokens and 10 ms. Without reuse, every call pays 160 ms before decode. With a hit on the system prompt, the call pays about 10 ms of prefill. You save 150 ms, which is 150 / 160 ≈ 94% of prefill, on the calls that hit. If half of calls hit, the average prefill falls from 160 ms to 0.5 × 160 + 0.5 × 10 = 85 ms. Decode of a 200-token answer at 5 ms is still about 1,000 ms. On that long answer, shaving prefill from 160 ms to 85 ms is real and secondary. On a classification call with no decode to speak of, it is the whole win.

What fails.

  • A tenant id is inserted at the start of the prompt and the shared prefix never hits.
  • Hit rate is not measured, so a full cache is assumed.
  • Eviction drops the popular prefix and keeps unique ones.
  • A decode-bound product is promised a 94% end-to-end win because prefill dropped 94%.

What you do. Measure hit rate and tokens skipped. Put shared text at the start of the prompt. Judge the win against end-to-end time, not against prefill alone.

prefill_miss_ms: 160
prefill_hit_ms: 10
hit_rate: 0.5
avg_prefill_ms: 85

articles.title: When the cache does not fit
articles.html:
Sometimes the working set does not fit. Long contexts, many concurrent sequences, or a prefix cache that retains too much will exhaust the reservation. The engine should reject or preempt before the kernel OOMs. A crash costs every caller on the replica. A refusal costs one caller and keeps the replica up.

You have three levers: admit fewer sequences, cap the length, or spill. Spilling cache to host memory saves the GPU and adds a stall when those tokens are read back. The stall can be worse than refusing the request and letting the client retry on a replica that has room. Measure the stall before you turn spill on as a default.

Mechanism. The allocator tracks free blocks. When a sequence needs a block and none are free, the scheduler either preempts a waiting sequence, evicts a prefix, spills, or fails the request. Preempting a sequence that was mid-decode throws away its cache and forces a recompute later. That is sometimes cheaper than spilling, and sometimes not. The policy belongs in the config you reviewed, not in a surprise default. Log which path you took. A replica that silently preempts every long request will show healthy GPUs and terrible tail latency.

Worked numbers. The GPU has 8 GB free for cache. A new request wants a 16,000-token context at about 256 MB per 2,048 tokens, so 16,000 / 2,048 × 256 MB = 7.8125 × 256 MB = 2,000 MB, about 2 GB. It fits in the 8 GB. Thirty such requests want about 60 GB and do not fit. If you admit all thirty, you will spill or crash. Admitting four uses about 8 GB and stays resident. Spilling the rest to host memory and reading a 2 GB cache back at 16 GB/s takes 2 / 16 = 0.125 s = 125 ms on the critical path, every time that sequence steps through spilled blocks. A 5 ms decode becomes a 125 ms stall when the cache is cold on the device. Refusal at admission is cleaner until you show the spill is rare and cheap.

What fails.

  • The replica OOMs and restarts, dropping every in-flight request.
  • Spill is on by default and tail latency tracks host bandwidth.
  • Preemption loops: a long request is evicted, recomputed, and evicted again.
  • The max length in the API is larger than any reservation you sized.

What you do. Set max length and max sequences so the resident working set fits. Fail admission when it does not. Turn on spill only with a measured stall and a cap on how much you will spill.

free_cache_gb: 8
one_long_gb: 2
admit: 4
spill_stall_ms: 125

problems.title: Half the bytes
problems.promptHtml: BF16 weights are 14 GB and the bandwidth floor is about 4.7 ms at 3,000 GB/s. INT8 streams about 7 GB. What is the new floor, and when would a 4.6 ms measurement tell you the kernel is not streaming 7 GB?
problems.answer: about 2.3 ms; 4.6 ms means you are still near the BF16 floor, so the bytes did not stay small.

problems.title: Slice
problems.promptHtml: The bar is 80. INT4 scores 79 overall and 61 on the numeric slice. The product is the numeric slice. Do you ship INT4, and by how many points does the slice miss?
problems.answer: no; the slice misses by 80 − 61 = 19 points.

problems.title: Hit savings
problems.promptHtml: A miss prefills in 160 ms and a hit prefills in 10 ms. Half of calls hit. What is the average prefill, and how many milliseconds of prefill did the average call save versus always missing?
problems.answer: 85 ms average; the save is 160 − 85 = 75 ms.

problems.title: Spill stall
problems.promptHtml: Reading a 2 GB spilled cache at 16 GB/s takes how many milliseconds, and why is that a different problem from a 5 ms resident decode step?
problems.answer: 2 / 16 = 0.125 s = 125 ms; the stall dwarfs the 5 ms step.

problems.title: Decode-bound win
problems.promptHtml: Prefix caching cuts average prefill from 160 ms to 85 ms. The answer is 200 tokens at 5 ms, about 1,000 ms of decode. Why is a "94% faster" claim, based on the hit's prefill, the wrong end-to-end story?
problems.answer: the 94% applies to prefill on hits, while end-to-end is dominated by about 1,000 ms of decode.

problems.title: Admit four
problems.promptHtml: Each long request needs about 2 GB of cache and you have 8 GB free. How many of those requests can stay fully resident, and what should you do with the fifth?
problems.answer: four; refuse or queue the fifth rather than OOM the replica.

problems.title: Prefill did not halve
problems.promptHtml: INT8 cuts weight bytes in half. Prefill is compute-bound at 80 ms with a 4.7 ms bandwidth floor. Decode is on the bandwidth floor. Which stage gets faster, and why does the prefill stay near 80 ms?
problems.answer: decode; prefill's roof is compute, so fewer weight bytes are not its ceiling.

problems.title: Do not move the bar
problems.promptHtml: INT8 scores 81 on the product slice against a bar of 80. A proposal lowers the bar to 75 so a faster INT4 at 61 can ship. Why do you refuse, and which artifact is already legal?
problems.answer: the bar is not edited to fit a technique; INT8 already clears 80.

bonus.title: Keep, reject, or measure
bonus.promptHtml: INT8 measures 2.5 ms against a 2.3 ms floor and scores 81 on the product slice with a bar of 80. INT4 would lower the floor to about 1.2 ms and scores 61 on that slice. Prefix caching raises hit rate but the first token of each prompt is a unique tenant id. What do you keep, what do you reject, and what do you fix before you judge the cache?
bonus.answer: keep INT8; reject INT4 on quality; move the shared prefix to the start so the cache can hit, then measure hit rate.

articles.title: Speculative decoding
articles.html:
Speculative decoding uses a cheap draft model to propose several tokens and a target model to check them in one pass. When the target agrees, you emit several tokens for about the cost of one target step. When it disagrees, you throw away the tail and pay the failed speculation. The win depends on how often the draft is right, and on the draft being actually cheap.

This is a latency technique for a single sequence's decode. It does not remove the need for the target weights. It can raise GPU work if you speculate poorly, because you ran a draft and a rejected check. Measure emitted tokens per target step, including the replacement, not the demo.

Mechanism. The draft produces K candidate tokens. The target runs a verify pass over those K tokens and accepts a prefix of the candidates that match what it would have sampled. The accepted prefix is emitted. The first rejected token is replaced with the target's own token, and the rest are dropped. If the draft is the same size as the target, you did not get a cheap proposal. If sampling is random and the draft does not match the target's distribution, the acceptance rate collapses. Temperature 0 is the easy case. High temperature is harder.

Worked numbers. A target step is 5 ms and produces 1 token, 200 tokens per second. A draft proposes 4 tokens in 1 ms, and the target verifies them in one 6 ms pass. Suppose the target accepts 3 of the 4 drafts. You also emit the target's replacement for the rejected token, so that is 4 tokens. You spent 1 + 6 = 7 ms to emit those 4, 7 / 4 = 1.75 ms per token, versus 5 ms before. Throughput per sequence is about 1,000 / 1.75 ≈ 570 tokens per second, a bit under 3×, if this acceptance holds. If the target accepts no drafts, you emit only the replacement: 7 ms for 1 token, slower than the plain 5 ms step. One accepted draft plus the replacement is 2 tokens in 7 ms, 3.5 ms each, which is still faster than 5 ms. Log emitted tokens per verify. Turn speculation off when that number is 1.

What fails.

  • The draft is almost as large as the target, so the "cheap" step is not cheap.
  • Acceptance is not logged, and a slower config stays on.
  • A high-temperature product is tuned with a temperature-0 demo.
  • Speculation is stacked on a bandwidth-bound batch job that was already full of useful work, and total GPU work goes up.

What you do. Report draft time, verify time, and emitted tokens per verify, counting the target's replacement, on the production sampling settings. Keep it when milliseconds per emitted token beat the plain target step.

target_ms: 5
draft_ms: 1
verify_ms: 6
accepted_drafts: 3
emitted: 4
ms_per_token: 1.75

articles.title: Parallelism
articles.html:
Tensor parallelism splits a layer across GPUs and communicates every layer. Pipeline parallelism assigns layers to stages and communicates between stages. Data parallelism, for serving, is just more replicas. Use more replicas when the model fits on one GPU and you need more slots. Use tensor or pipeline parallelism when the model does not fit, or when a measured split beats one GPU on the contract you care about.

The hardware chapter already showed a split that made a fitting model slower. This lesson is the serving version: pick the parallel plan from fit and from bytes on the link, then confirm with the benchmark contract.

Mechanism. Tensor parallelism cuts per-GPU memory for the sharded weights and adds an all-reduce or all-gather each layer. Pipeline parallelism cuts memory by holding fewer layers per GPU and adds a bubble when a stage waits for the previous stage. Bubbles get worse when the batch is small, which is exactly the latency-sensitive case. Replicas avoid both, at the cost of a full copy of the weights on every GPU. If the weights fit, replicas are the default. Sharding is what you do so that a model which does not fit can run at all.

Worked numbers. A model needs 140 GB of weights. One 80 GB GPU cannot hold it. Two GPUs with tensor parallelism hold about 70 GB of weights each, plus cache, which fits in 80 GB if the cache is modest. The link exchange was about 8 ms in the earlier example. A single step cannot be faster than that exchange if it is on the critical path, but the alternative is not running the model. Compare 8 ms with the product budget, not with a mythical one-GPU 70B BF16 that does not fit. If you only needed more copies of a 14 GB model, two replicas give you two batches and no 8 ms tax. Sharding that 14 GB model "for speed" pays the tax for nothing.

What fails.

  • Tensor parallelism is enabled on a model that already fits, and latency rises.
  • Pipeline parallelism is used at batch 1, and the bubble dominates.
  • A 140 GB model is given one 80 GB GPU and the OOM is called a kernel bug.
  • Replicas are sharded across boxes with a slow network because the scheduler ignored the link.

What you do. If it fits, add replicas. If it does not, shard on a fast link and put the exchange floor next to the latency budget before you promise a speedup.

weights_gb: 140
gpus: 2
per_gpu_gb: 70
link_floor_ms: 8
reason: fit

articles.title: Disaggregation
articles.html:
Disaggregation runs prefill and decode on different pools. Prefill wants compute and can use a batch of prompts. Decode wants bandwidth and a lot of cache, and it runs for a long time per request. Separating them stops a long prefill from stalling a decode pool, and it lets you buy different GPUs for each roof. The cost is moving the KV cache from the prefill GPU to the decode GPU.

If that transfer is slower than the time you saved, you made the architecture diagram nicer and the request slower. The transfer has to be measured on the network you have.

Mechanism. A request prefills on a prefill worker. The cache is sent to a decode worker, which generates tokens until the sequence ends. The scheduler has to place the cache where there is room and keep the two pools sized for the mix. Too few prefill workers and time to first token grows. Too few decode workers and inter-token time grows. The cache transfer sits on the path between those clocks. A shared pool with chunked prefill is the alternative when the transfer is expensive and the mix is mild. Disaggregation is the alternative when the two stages fight and the network can move the cache in time.

Worked numbers. A 2,048-token cache is about 256 MB. On a 10 GB/s network the copy takes 0.256 / 10 = 0.0256 s ≈ 26 ms. Prefill was 80 ms and the first decode steps were being delayed by that full 80 ms on a shared GPU. Moving prefill off the decode GPU removes that stall, and the 26 ms transfer can be cheaper than an 80 ms interruption. If the network is 1 GB/s, the copy takes about 256 ms, which is worse than staying together and chunking the prefill into 15 ms slices. Do the division before you split the fleet.

What fails.

  • Pools are split and the cache copy takes longer than the stall it removed.
  • Prefill capacity and decode capacity are scaled together even though the mix changed.
  • The transfer is assumed to be HBM speed because both GPUs are "in the cloud."
  • Disaggregation is turned on for a short-prompt, short-answer route that never stalled.

What you do. Measure cache bytes and network bandwidth. Split the pools when the copy is cheaper than the interference. Size the pools from prefill arrivals and decode slots separately.

cache_mb: 256
net_gb_s: 10
copy_ms: 26
shared_stall_ms: 80

articles.title: Choose the first technique
articles.html:
You do not apply quantization, speculation, parallelism, and disaggregation in one change. You name the roof that is hurting, pick the technique that moves that roof, and leave the others off. The measurement contract and the quality bar decide whether it stays.

A sensible order for a chat model that fits on one GPU: batch in an engine, then quantize weights if decode is bandwidth-bound and the eval passes, then prefix caching if prefill repeats, then speculation if a single stream is still too slow, then replicas for concurrency. Shard or disaggregate when the fit or the interference says you must. Skipping ahead is how four knobs move and no result is real.

Mechanism. Write the bottleneck in one line, from the model and hardware chapters: bandwidth-bound decode, compute-bound prefill, cache that does not fit, or a model that does not fit. Match a technique to that line. Run the frozen benchmark twice on the baseline, once on the candidate, and the frozen eval on the candidate. Ship only if latency, quality, and cost all still fit the budgets. Queue the next technique behind that ship. A roadmap that turns every technique on is not a roadmap. It is an unreviewed config.

Worked numbers. Decode measures 5.1 ms against a 4.7 ms BF16 floor. INT8's floor is 2.3 ms and a trial measures 2.5 ms with a score of 81 against a bar of 80. That is the first technique. Speculation might take you from 2.5 ms toward about 0.9 ms per token if you emit 4 tokens for every 7 ms of draft and verify, as in the earlier example, and it is the second experiment, not a simultaneous one. Tensor parallelism on this 14 GB model is not on the list, because it fits. A teammate who wants all four flags on today cannot tell you whether the eval drop came from INT4, from the grammar in the speculative sampler, or from a bad shard. One flag, one result.

What fails.

  • Four techniques land in one release and quality drops.
  • A technique is applied to a stage whose roof it does not move.
  • The order starts with sharding a model that fits.
  • A win on a demo sampling setting is shipped at a different temperature.

What you do. One bottleneck sentence, one technique, one rerun of the contract and the eval. Then the next technique.

bottleneck: decode bandwidth
first: int8
measured_ms: 2.5
quality: 81
bar: 80

problems.title: Accepted tokens
problems.promptHtml: Draft is 1 ms, verify is 6 ms, and the target accepts 3 of 4 draft tokens, then emits its replacement for the rejected one. How many tokens do you emit, and how many milliseconds do you spend per emitted token, compared with a plain 5 ms target step?
problems.answer: 4 tokens; 7 / 4 = 1.75 ms per token, faster than 5 ms.

problems.title: Acceptance collapses
problems.promptHtml: The same 7 ms path accepts no draft tokens and emits only the target's replacement. Are you faster or slower than the plain 5 ms step, and what do you turn off?
problems.answer: slower, 7 ms for one token versus 5 ms; turn speculation off.

problems.title: Why two GPUs
problems.promptHtml: Weights are 140 GB and one GPU has 80 GB. Two GPUs hold about 70 GB each. Why is this split justified even if the link floor is 8 ms?
problems.answer: the model does not fit on one GPU; the alternative is not a faster single card, it is failing to load.

problems.title: Copy versus stall
problems.promptHtml: A 256 MB cache copy at 10 GB/s takes about 26 ms. A shared GPU stalls decode for an 80 ms prefill. Is the split cheaper than the stall on this network? What if the network is 1 GB/s?
problems.answer: yes at 10 GB/s, 26 ms is under 80 ms; at 1 GB/s the copy is about 256 ms, which is worse.

problems.title: Replicas not shards
problems.promptHtml: A 14 GB model fits and you need more concurrent chats. Why are extra replicas the default, and what tax does tensor parallelism add that replicas do not?
problems.answer: each replica is an independent batch; tensor parallelism adds a per-layer link exchange.

problems.title: First flag
problems.promptHtml: Decode is 5.1 ms against a 4.7 ms floor. INT8 measures 2.5 ms and scores 81 against a bar of 80. Why is this the technique you ship before speculation or sharding?
problems.answer: it moves the bandwidth roof and clears the bar; speculation is a later experiment and sharding is unnecessary because the model fits.

problems.title: Four flags
problems.promptHtml: Quality falls after a release that enabled INT4, speculation at high temperature, and a two-GPU shard of a model that already fit. Why can you not name the cause, and what is the rollback?
problems.answer: three techniques moved at once; roll back to the last single-technique digest that cleared the eval.

problems.title: When speculation wastes the GPU
problems.promptHtml: A batch job is already filling the GPU with useful decode at a high acceptance of real user tokens. Adding a draft that often misses increases GPU work per accepted token. Why can speculation lower throughput here even though it helped a single-stream latency demo?
problems.answer: rejected drafts spend GPU time that was already busy with useful tokens; the demo was one idle stream, the batch job was full.

bonus.title: Match the technique
bonus.promptHtml: Name the first technique for each bottleneck: a bandwidth-bound BF16 decode that passes an INT8 eval, a long prefill that blocks other decodes on a fast network where a 256 MB copy takes about 26 ms against an 80 ms stall, and a 140 GB model on 80 GB cards. Say which one is not "add tensor parallelism" of a model that already fits.
bonus.answer: INT8 for the decode; disaggregation for the prefill interference; shard the 140 GB model so it fits; do not shard a model that already fits.

articles.title: Vision-language models
articles.html:
A vision-language model takes images and text and produces text. The image is encoded into tokens or embeddings, then the language model runs a prefill over that mixed sequence and decodes an answer. The new cost is the vision encoder and the length of the visual tokens. A high-resolution image can be more tokens than the user's question. Time to first token includes the encoder plus that prefill.

The language half is the language half. KV cache, quantization, and speculative decoding still apply to the decode. They do not apply to the encoder until you show the encoder is the same kind of kernel. Often it is a separate tower with its own weights and its own roof.

Mechanism. Pixels are resized, patched, and run through the vision tower. The tower emits a sequence of visual tokens. Those tokens are prefixed or interleaved with text tokens. The language model prefills the combined sequence and then decodes. Caching the vision result for a repeated image is the analogue of prefix caching. A new image misses. A new question about the same image can hit if you stored the visual tokens. Memory has to hold the vision weights and the language weights, or you run them on different devices and pay a transfer.

Worked numbers. The vision tower takes 40 ms and emits 1,000 visual tokens. Language prefill is 80 ms per 1,024 text tokens, so about 80 ms for those 1,000 visual tokens. A short question rides in that same prefill. It is not a second 80 ms. Decode of a 50-token answer at 5 ms is 250 ms. Time to first token is about 40 + 80 = 120 ms before decode, and the answer ends near 120 + 250 = 370 ms if decode starts immediately. Someone who budgets only the text question, 20 tokens, will predict a tiny prefill and miss by the visual tokens. Count visual tokens in the length bucket.

What fails.

  • Latency is planned from the text length and the image is ignored.
  • Vision weights are forgotten in the fit test, and the replica OOMs only when an image arrives.
  • A text quant is applied to the vision tower without an image eval.
  • The same image is re-encoded on every question in a thread.

What you do. Put visual tokens in the length metric. Fit both towers. Cache the encoder output for a repeated image. Run an eval that includes images, not only text.

vision_ms: 40
visual_tokens: 1000
prefill_ms: 80
decode_ms: 250

articles.title: Embeddings
articles.html:
Embedding models map a text or an image to a vector. There is usually no token stream to the caller. The request is a batch of inputs, and the response is a batch of vectors. Throughput is vectors per second. Latency is time to the whole batch, or time to one document if you serve interactively. A chat engine with a KV cache and a decode loop is the wrong shape. You want a batched forward of the encoder and a pooler.

Quality is whether nearest neighbors are still right. A quant that keeps chat fluent can move vectors enough to break retrieval. The eval is a retrieval set, not a summary set.

Mechanism. Tokenize a batch of documents, run the encoder once, pool the token states into one vector per document, and normalize if the index expects it. There is no autoregressive loop, so the GPU can take a large batch and stay compute-bound. The index that stores the vectors is a separate system. You can be fast at embedding and still be slow at search if the index is the ceiling. Say which one you own. Re-embedding a corpus is an offline job with a deadline. Embedding the user's query is online and sits on the search path.

Worked numbers. One GPU embeds 2,000 documents per second at batch 64. A corpus of 20 million documents takes 20,000,000 / 2,000 = 10,000 seconds, about 10,000 / 3,600 ≈ 2.8 hours on one GPU. That is an offline job for one card, if the card stays up. The query path embeds one short string in 15 ms and then the index takes 20 ms. The user's wait is 35 ms, and buying a faster embedding GPU saves at most 15 ms. Do not size the query SLO as if it were the corpus rebuild. Do not size the rebuild as if it were a 15 ms call.

What fails.

  • Embeddings are served through a chat decode loop.
  • A chat quality eval blesses a quant that breaks neighbors.
  • The corpus rebuild and the query path share one latency budget.
  • The index time is blamed on the encoder.

What you do. Batch the encoder. Eval with retrieval. Split offline rebuild throughput from online query latency, and add the index time to the query budget.

docs_per_s: 2000
corpus: 20000000
rebuild_hours: 2.8
query_embed_ms: 15
index_ms: 20

articles.title: Speech recognition
articles.html:
Automatic speech recognition turns audio into text. The input size is seconds of audio, not tokens, until the encoder produces frames. Streaming recognition emits partial text while the person is still talking. Batch recognition waits for the file. They share a model and not a deadline. Streaming cares about how late the partial is relative to the audio. Batch cares about audio-hours per GPU-hour.

Many modern ASR stacks are close to a transformer over frames. Frame rate sets the sequence length. A 30-second clip at 50 frames per second is 1,500 frames, a long prefill, not a chat prompt. Do not cap "tokens" at 512 and then wonder why audio fails admission.

Mechanism. Audio is windowed into frames, encoded, and decoded into text. Streaming keeps a state over the frames seen so far and updates the transcript. That state is the cache. A long meeting is a long sequence. Endpointing decides when an utterance ended. A bad endpoint cuts the user off or holds the GPU for silence. The decoder may be a small language model that cleans up tokens. Its cost can be hidden until the audio encoder got fast.

Worked numbers. A clip produces 50 frames per second. A 30-second utterance is 1,500 frames. If the encoder runs at 100 ms per second of audio, the 30-second clip costs 3 seconds of GPU time after it has fully arrived, a real-time factor of 3 / 30 = 0.1, so you are ten times faster than real time and one GPU can keep up with about 10 concurrent streams if they are this shape. Streaming partials that must appear within 200 ms of speech cannot wait for the whole 30 seconds. You run every few hundred milliseconds of new audio. A batch file of the same 30 seconds can wait and take a bigger batch. The concurrent-stream math and the overnight-file math are different admission policies.

What fails.

  • A chat max-sequence setting rejects audio frames.
  • Streaming and batch share a queue, so a long file delays partials.
  • Silence never endpoints, and a stream holds a cache all afternoon.
  • Real-time factor is reported on a GPU and the CPU resample is the actual ceiling.

What you do. Size sequence length in frames. Separate streaming admission from batch files. Endpoint silence. Include resample and feature time in the trace.

frames_per_s: 50
utt_s: 30
frames: 1500
rtf: 0.1
streams_per_gpu: 10

articles.title: Speech synthesis
articles.html:
Text-to-speech turns text into audio. The caller may want the first audio chunk quickly and the rest streamed, which is the analogue of time to first token and inter-token time. The "token" might be a frame of waveform or a codec code. Quality is listening, or a frozen set of intelligibility and speaker similarity scores. A faster vocoder that sounds like a different person is a failed eval.

The model may be two stages: an acoustic model that predicts features, and a vocoder that predicts waveform. Either stage can be the roof. Measure them separately before you optimize the one you can see in a profiler screenshot.

Mechanism. Text is normalized and phonemized or tokenized, then the acoustic model generates a sequence of frames, then the vocoder renders audio. Streaming sends audio chunks as frames are ready. The first-chunk latency includes text processing plus the first frames. A long sentence does not need to finish before the caller hears the start, if you stream. GPU memory holds the model and the frames in flight. A batch of unrelated utterances can share the vocoder the way a decode batch shares weights, if their frame sizes are managed.

Worked numbers. The first audio chunk takes 120 ms of model time. Later audio is produced at 20 ms of GPU time per 100 ms of audio, a real-time factor of 0.2, so one stream is easy and one GPU can cover about 5 such streams before it is out of compute, if the 20 ms is the limit. The product needs the first chunk under 200 ms and no underrun after that. You are inside 200 ms on the first chunk. The budget for the scheduler between chunks is the audio duration minus the GPU time, 100 − 20 = 80 ms of slack. A batching wait of 90 ms plus the 20 ms of GPU time is 110 ms, which underruns the 100 ms of audio you owe. A wait of 150 ms underruns by more. Do not copy a chat batch cap that waits longer than that 80 ms slack.

What fails.

  • First-chunk latency is ignored and only overall throughput is tuned.
  • The vocoder is sped up and speaker similarity falls through the bar.
  • Scheduler waits exceed the slack and the audio underruns.
  • Text normalization on the CPU is outside the trace and dominates the 120 ms.

What you do. Budget first chunk and inter-chunk slack separately. Eval speaker and intelligibility on the frozen set. Trace the CPU text front end.

first_chunk_ms: 120
gpu_ms_per_100ms_audio: 20
slack_ms: 80
budget_first_ms: 200

problems.title: Count the image
problems.promptHtml: The vision tower takes 40 ms and emits 1,000 tokens. Language prefill of that sequence is 80 ms. A budget built from a 20-token question ignored the image. What is time to first token from these two stages alone?
problems.answer: 40 + 80 = 120 ms, and the visual tokens dominate the question.

problems.title: Rebuild versus query
