problems.promptHtml: One GPU embeds 2,000 documents per second. How long is a 20 million document rebuild, in hours? The query path is 15 ms of embedding plus 20 ms of index. How much of the query can a faster encoder remove?
problems.answer: about 2.8 hours; at most the 15 ms, not the 20 ms index.

problems.title: Real-time factor
problems.promptHtml: Thirty seconds of audio costs 3 seconds of GPU time. What is the real-time factor, and about how many such streams can one GPU keep up with?
problems.answer: 3 / 30 = 0.1; about 10 streams.

problems.title: Slack
problems.promptHtml: Each 100 ms of audio costs 20 ms of GPU time. The product cannot underrun. How much scheduler slack do you have between chunks, and does a 150 ms wait fit?
problems.answer: 80 ms of slack; a 150 ms wait underruns.

problems.title: Wrong eval
problems.promptHtml: A quantized embedding model still scores well on a chat summary set and retrieval recall falls off a cliff. Why was the chat set the wrong gate?
problems.answer: embeddings are judged by neighbors or retrieval, not by summary quality.

problems.title: Same image
problems.promptHtml: A thread asks three questions about one image. The vision tower is 40 ms. How many milliseconds do you waste by re-encoding every question, and what do you cache instead?
problems.answer: 2 extra encodes, 80 ms; cache the visual tokens for that image.

problems.title: Two policies
problems.promptHtml: Streaming ASR must emit partials within 200 ms of speech. A batch transcription job can wait until morning. Why do they not share one admission queue, even on the same weights?
problems.answer: streaming is a latency queue and batch files would block partials; separate admission the way online and offline text serving do.

problems.title: Both towers
problems.promptHtml: Language weights are 14 GB and fit. Vision weights are another 8 GB, and the max visual cache pushes the total to 78 GB on an 80 GB card. A text-only dry-load succeeds. Why does the first real image request still OOM, and what dry-load would have caught it?
problems.answer: the text dry-load never allocated the vision tower and the visual cache; dry-load an image at max resolution.

bonus.title: Which clock
bonus.promptHtml: For a vision-language request, an embedding query, and a streaming TTS call, name the first clock you would put on the dashboard: time to first token including the vision tower, embedding milliseconds plus index milliseconds, or first-chunk latency and inter-chunk slack.
bonus.answer: vision-language uses time to first token including the encoder; embeddings use embed time plus index time; TTS uses first chunk and the slack between chunks.

articles.title: Diffusion steps
articles.html:
Diffusion and its cousins generate an image by iterating a denoiser. Each step is a forward pass. The caller usually needs the finished image, so latency is steps times time per step, plus a decoder. Quality moves with step count, sampler, resolution, and the checkpoint. You already saw the arithmetic in the model chapter. Here it becomes the serving config: the step count is a product setting with an eval, not a hidden constant.

A lower step count is the first technique, the way fewer bytes was the first technique for decode. It is also the easiest way to ship a worse image. The frozen eval is a set of prompts with a score a human or a model judge can repeat. You do not "know it is fine" from one picture on your laptop.

Mechanism. Sample noise, run N denoiser steps, decode the latent to pixels. The server should expose N and the resolution as request parameters with hard caps. A cap is what keeps one caller from asking for 200 steps at 4K and pinning the GPU. Batch together requests that share resolution and step count when you can. Mixed sizes waste the batch. The weights stay resident. The latent for each image is the per-request state, analogous to a cache and much shorter-lived.

Worked numbers. One step is 40 ms at 512 pixels. The eval passes at 20 steps and fails at 10. Twenty steps cost 800 ms, plus 50 ms to decode, 850 ms. Thirty steps would cost 1,200 ms plus 50 ms and also pass, and you do not buy the extra 400 ms. Ten steps cost 400 ms and fail the eval, so you do not ship them to make a demo feel quick. The allowed config is 20 steps at this resolution. Put that in the API default and reject 80-step requests or put them on a batch queue with a different deadline.

What fails.

  • Step count is cut and the eval is a single screenshot.
  • Clients can request unbounded steps.
  • Mixed resolutions are forced into one batch and the pack is awful.
  • The 30-step setting stays as the default after 20 steps already passes.

What you do. Freeze an image eval. Set the default step count to the smallest N that passes. Cap the maximum N and the maximum resolution.

step_ms: 40
steps_pass: 20
e2e_ms: 850
steps_fail: 10

articles.title: Image serving
articles.html:
Serving images is a request-response or a slow stream of previews. There is no inter-token budget. There is queue time, denoise time, and decode time. Interactive apps need a latency cap. Offline generation of a catalog can use a big batch and a deadline. The same weights can sit behind both, on separate queues, as with online and offline text.

Cold start includes loading a checkpoint that may be several gigabytes plus a VAE decoder. A scale-from-zero design pays that load on the first picture. Preview models and final models are sometimes different checkpoints. Do not time one and advertise the other.

Mechanism. The gateway authenticates and checks the cap on resolution and steps. The scheduler groups compatible jobs. The runner executes the steps and the decoder and returns bytes, or object-storage URLs if the payload is large. Returning a multi-megabyte image through a tiny synchronous response can time out at the proxy even when the GPU finished. Know which hop carries the bytes. Metrics are images per second at a stated resolution and step count, and p95 end-to-end at a stated concurrency.

Worked numbers. The GPU path is 850 ms. A proxy timeout is 1,000 ms. The image is 4 MB and the proxy path you measured moves 8 MB/s, so the upload takes 4 / 8 = 0.5 s = 500 ms. Total is 850 + 500 = 1,350 ms, which misses the proxy. The GPU was fast enough. The bytes were not. Write the image to object storage and return a URL, or raise the proxy timeout, or shrink the payload. A kernel change does not move the 500 ms. At concurrency 1 the GPU does about 1 / 0.85 ≈ 1.2 images per second. A catalog of 100,000 images takes 100,000 / 1.2 ≈ 83,000 seconds, about 23 hours on one GPU. That is an offline queue.

What fails.

  • Proxy timeout is blamed on the denoiser while the body upload is the miss.
  • Interactive and catalog jobs share a queue.
  • Images per second is quoted with no resolution and no step count.
  • Scale-from-zero is promised for a 5-second weight load inside a 1-second budget.

What you do. Split clocks into queue, denoise, decode, and byte transfer. Return a URL when the body is the problem. Keep a separate offline queue for the catalog.

gpu_ms: 850
upload_ms: 500
proxy_ms: 1000
miss: upload

articles.title: Video serving
articles.html:
Video is many frames. A naive reading is image cost times frames, and that is the right first estimate. Real systems amortize some work across frames and still scale badly with duration, resolution, and frame rate. A 4-second clip at 8 frames per second is 32 frames. If each frame were an independent 850 ms image, the clip would be 27 seconds of GPU time, which is a different product from chat and a different product from one picture.

Streaming a video before it is finished is possible and is still not token streaming. You have a buffer of frames to encode into a container the player accepts. The player will underrun if you miss the frame deadline. The slack math from speech synthesis shows up again, with a heavier step.

Mechanism. Generate frames in order, sometimes conditioned on the previous frame, then encode them into a compressed video. Conditioning means you cannot always batch independent frames of one clip the way you batch independent images. Multiple clips can still share the GPU. Memory holds several frames of latent state. A longer clip or a higher resolution can OOM a config that was fine for a 16-frame preview. Cap duration, resolution, and frame rate the way you cap sequence length.

Worked numbers. A preview is 16 frames at 200 ms of model time each, 3.2 seconds of GPU time, plus 0.3 seconds to encode, 3.5 seconds. A requested clip of 64 frames is 12.8 seconds plus encode, about 13 seconds. If the API leaves duration unbounded, one caller asks for 10 seconds at 24 frames per second, 240 frames, about 48 seconds of GPU time before encode. That single request occupies the replica for most of a minute. Cap duration at the preview you evaluated, or send long clips to the offline queue with a price. Do not let one video request sit in the interactive queue in front of image requests that take 850 ms.

What fails.

  • Duration is uncapped on the interactive queue.
  • Frame cost is assumed independent when the model conditions on the previous frame and the batch plan is wrong.
  • A 16-frame preview budget is advertised for a 240-frame request.
  • The video encoder on the CPU is omitted, and the GPU looks idle at the end of every clip.

What you do. Estimate GPU time as frames times time per frame, plus encode. Cap the interactive duration. Trace the encoder.

frame_ms: 200
preview_frames: 16
preview_s: 3.2
uncapped_frames: 240

articles.title: Do not copy the chat config
articles.html:
Chat config carries max sequence length, KV cache blocks, time to first token, and inter-token slack. Image and video config carries steps, resolution, frame count, and a deadline for the finished artifact or the next frame. Copying the chat config onto a pixel route leaves the real caps unset and sets caps that do nothing. Copying a pixel config onto chat does the reverse.

The engine can be different. A diffusion runtime is not a paged-attention runtime. Sharing a process because "it is all inference" couples their queues and their failures. Separate processes, separate queues, separate dashboards. Share the platform habits: a frozen eval, a measurement contract, a fit test, and one technique at a time.

Mechanism. Write the per-route config explicitly. Chat: max tokens, cache reservation, p95 time to first token, p95 inter-token time. Image: max steps, max side length, p95 time to image. Video: max frames, max side, p95 time to clip or max real-time factor. A deploy that changes a global default changes every route. Prefer a default per route so a video cap cannot shrink the chat context, and a chat context bump cannot raise the video frame cap. On a page, the route name is the first word, then the clock that belongs to that route.

Worked numbers. A global timeout of 2,000 ms fits many chat answers and fails a 16-frame preview at 3.5 seconds. Someone raises the global timeout to 30 seconds so video works. Chat clients now wait 30 seconds before they retry a dead replica, and a hung text request holds a slot that the 2,000 ms budget was supposed to free. The video route needed its own 10-second budget. The chat route needed to keep 2,000 ms. One global number made both wrong. Split them.

What fails.

  • One timeout serves chat and video.
  • KV cache settings are tuned on a diffusion process that has no KV cache.
  • A video frame cap is raised in a shared config and chat memory reservations change with it.
  • An incident channel has one latency chart for every modality.

What you do. One config block and one dashboard per route. Keep the platform habits. Do not keep the same knobs.

chat_timeout_ms: 2000
video_timeout_ms: 10000
shared_global_timeout: no

problems.title: Smallest passing N
problems.promptHtml: Steps cost 40 ms. The eval passes at 20 steps and fails at 10. What is the model time you ship, and why do you not ship 10 steps to save 400 ms?
problems.answer: 20 × 40 = 800 ms; 10 steps fail the eval.

problems.title: Upload
problems.promptHtml: The GPU finishes in 850 ms. Uploading a 4 MB image at 8 MB/s takes 500 ms. A proxy allows 1,000 ms. Does the request make it, and which hop do you fix first?
problems.answer: no, 1,350 ms total; fix the byte transfer, not the denoiser.

problems.title: Sixteen frames
problems.promptHtml: Each frame costs 200 ms. A preview is 16 frames. How many seconds of GPU time is the preview, before the encoder?

problems.title: Uncapped
problems.promptHtml: One interactive request asks for 240 frames at 200 ms each. How many seconds of GPU time is that, and why does it not belong in front of an 850 ms image queue?
problems.answer: 48 seconds; it blocks many interactive images, so cap it or send it offline.

problems.title: Global timeout
problems.promptHtml: Chat was budgeted at 2,000 ms. A 16-frame video preview takes 3.5 seconds. Someone sets a global timeout of 30 seconds. What breaks for chat, and what should you set instead?
problems.answer: chat clients wait too long to retry and slots stay busy; give video its own timeout and keep chat at 2,000 ms.

problems.title: Catalog
problems.promptHtml: One GPU produces about 1.2 images per second at the shipped step count. How long does a catalog of 100,000 images take on one GPU, in hours, and which queue is that?
problems.answer: 100,000 / 1.2 ≈ 83,000 seconds, about 23 hours; the offline queue.

problems.title: No KV here
problems.promptHtml: A diffusion service is slow. A teammate imports the chat engine's KV cache flags and paged-attention settings. Why is that the wrong layer, and which two caps should they set instead?
problems.answer: diffusion spends time on denoising steps, not a token cache; cap steps and resolution.

problems.title: Encoder
problems.promptHtml: GPU frame time accounts for 3.2 seconds of a preview. The trace says the replica stays busy for 3.5 seconds and the GPU is idle for the last 0.3 seconds. Where did the 0.3 seconds go, and why is a denoiser kernel the wrong first edit?
problems.answer: the video encoder, often on the CPU; the denoiser already finished.

bonus.title: Separate routes
bonus.promptHtml: You run chat, a single-image API, and a video API. Chat p95 time to first token is the product clock. Images are 20 steps at 40 ms plus upload. Video previews are 16 frames at 200 ms. Give each route its clock and one cap that must not be global. Say why a single 30-second timeout is not the cap.
bonus.answer: chat uses time to first token and a short timeout; images use step count, resolution, and time to image; video uses frame count and its own longer timeout; one 30-second timeout makes chat retries late and still may not fit a long video.

articles.title: A container and a replica
articles.html:
A replica is a container image plus a GPU, a command, and a readiness check. The image pins the engine, the driver libraries it needs, and the startup script. The command pins the digest, the max length, and the port. Readiness passes only after the dry-load finishes and the process can answer a tiny request. A process that has bound a port and has not loaded weights is not ready.

One replica should be boring and replaceable. You do not SSH in to fix it. You roll the image or the command. If a replica is special, the next one you add will not match it, and the fleet will drift.

Mechanism. The scheduler places the container on a node with a free GPU of the SKU you asked for. The process loads the artifact, allocates the cache pool, and then flips ready. The balancer watches ready, not merely running. A liveness check restarts a process that is wedged. A readiness check removes a process that is alive but should not take traffic, for example during a long load. Mixing those two checks means you restart replicas that were simply still loading, or you keep sending traffic to replicas that are wedged.

Worked numbers. Cold load of a 14 GB artifact at 3 GB/s is about 4.7 s, plus 2 s of runtime init, about 6.7 s before ready. A liveness timeout of 3 s will kill the process during every boot and it will never become ready. Set liveness to tolerate startup, or use a startup probe that allows 30 s and a liveness probe that only starts after ready. Once ready, a health check that runs a 1-token generate every 10 s costs a little GPU and catches a wedge that a TCP check would miss. A TCP check alone stays green while the engine is stuck in a CUDA error. Prefer a generate that is cheaper than a real user request and frequent enough that a wedge does not sit in the balancer for minutes.

What fails.

  • Readiness is "the port is open."
  • Liveness kills the container during weight load.
  • The image floats on a tag that moved since yesterday.
  • One replica was hand-patched and cannot be reproduced.

What you do. Pin the image digest and the model digest. Ready means a successful tiny generate. Let startup take longer than the load time you measured.

image: engine@sha256:abc
model: run-1842
startup_s: 30
ready: tiny generate

articles.title: Autoscaling
articles.html:
Scale on the signal that means you are short of slots: queue time, or concurrent requests divided by what a ready replica can hold. Scaling on CPU, or on GPU utilization alone, will lie. A bandwidth-bound decode can sit at modest compute utilization and still be at its latency roof. A stuck replica can show high utilization while it serves nobody useful.

Scale in is as dangerous as scale out. Dropping a replica that holds long contexts throws away caches and pushes prefill onto the survivors. Scale in slowly, and drain before you kill.

Mechanism. The autoscaler reads a metric, compares it with a target, and changes the desired replica count. Desired is not ready. New replicas take the startup time from the previous lesson before they add capacity. A spike shorter than startup cannot be met by scaling from zero. Hold a warm floor. When scaling in, mark the replica not-ready, wait for in-flight requests to finish or hit a drain timeout, then stop it. A hard kill mid-decode makes those callers retry on the remaining replicas and can cause a second spike.

Worked numbers. Each ready replica handles 10 requests per second inside the budget. You want headroom, so you target 7 per replica. Arrivals are 28 per second. You want 28 / 7 = 4 ready replicas. You have 4, and one is about to scale in because a one-minute average dipped. The next minute is 40 per second, which wants 40 / 7 ≈ 6 replicas. Startup is 6.7 s, so those 2 replicas are late but useful. If you had scaled to zero, the whole 6.7 s would be a brownout. If the dip-to-3 happens anyway, capacity falls to 3 × 10 = 30 per second just as 40 arrive. The queue grows. Scale-in policy should require the lower load to last longer than a burst, and longer than startup, before it removes a replica.

What fails.

  • The metric is GPU utilization and the scaler removes replicas that were bandwidth-bound and busy enough.
  • Scale-from-zero is the plan for a chat SLO inside the startup time.
  • Scale-in kills connections without draining.
  • Desired count is paged, and unready replicas look like capacity.

What you do. Scale on queue or on arrivals per ready replica. Keep a warm floor. Drain on the way down. Alert when ready stays below desired for longer than startup.

arrivals_per_s: 28
target_per_replica: 7
want_ready: 4
startup_s: 6.7
floor: 2

articles.title: More than one region
articles.html:
A second region is a second fleet with its own replicas, its own artifact cache, and its own failure domain. You add it for latency to users, or for survival when one region dies. You do not add it because a chart was noisy. Each region has to load the digest, pass readiness, and receive only the traffic it can serve. A global balancer that sends everyone to the nearest region will overload a small region that happens to be near a big user base.

Failover is a tested path, not a hope. If you have never shifted traffic, you do not have a second region. You have a second bill.

Mechanism. Users hit a global entry that picks a region by health and by load, not only by ping. Each region reports ready capacity. The entry stops sending to a region that fails its health check. Data that must exist in both places is the model artifact and the config, not the KV cache. Caches are local. A user who fails over mid-conversation pays prefill again. That is acceptable. A user who fails over and hits a region that never pulled the digest is not. Replication of the artifact is a deploy step, ahead of traffic.

Worked numbers. Region A has 6 ready replicas. Region B has 2. A nearest-region policy sends 80% of traffic to B because the users are there. B can take 2 × 10 = 20 requests per second. The 80% is 40 requests per second, so the other 20% is 10 requests per second on A. B is short by a factor of two. A is underused: it can take 6 × 10 = 60 per second and is only serving 10. The balancer should cap B at its ready capacity and spill the extra 20 per second to A, paying a few tens of milliseconds of network instead of a queue. When A dies, B cannot absorb 100% unless you have kept B large enough, or you shed load. Write that down before the outage. A failover plan that needs B to suddenly have A's 6 replicas will wait through image pulls and the 6.7 s startup, times however many nodes you can get.

What fails.

  • Nearest-region routing ignores ready capacity.
  • The artifact exists only in one region's storage.
  • Failover is designed during the incident.
  • KV caches are expected to replicate across the ocean.

What you do. Route by health and capacity. Replicate artifacts before you announce the region. Practice a failover when nothing is on fire.

region_a_ready: 6
region_b_ready: 2
b_cap_rps: 20
b_demand_rps: 40
spill_to_a: 20

articles.title: A deploy you can undo
articles.html:
A deploy changes one thing: the image, the digest, or a config knob. It rolls forward one replica or a small percent, watches the clocks and the eval canary, and then continues. If the clocks move the wrong way, it stops and returns to the previous pin. The previous pin has to still be running or still be loadable. Deleting it as part of the deploy removes the undo.

Canary traffic should look like real traffic. A canary that only receives your manual prompts will bless a regression on the long-prompt slice. Send it a fraction of production, or a replay of the frozen benchmark, and compare percentiles with the baseline replicas.

Mechanism. The rollout controller starts N new replicas, waits until they are ready, shifts a slice of traffic, and compares error rate and latency with the old replicas over a window long enough to see a tail. Then it shifts more. A failure threshold aborts and shifts traffic back. Config and image are versioned with the model digest so the undo is a pointer move, not a rebuild. Database migrations and other irreversible steps do not belong in the same change as an engine bump. You want the engine bump to be reversible in one action.

Worked numbers. Baseline p95 time to first token is 200 ms. The canary, at 5% of traffic, measures 260 ms over ten minutes, with errors flat. The budget is 220 ms. You abort. The 60 ms gap is larger than the 6 ms noise band from the benchmark chapter. Shift traffic back to the old digest. If you had rolled 100% first, every user would eat the 260 ms until you noticed. Five percent for ten minutes limits the damage. A canary that is "green" because errors are zero and nobody looked at p95 would have promoted a latency regression. Both gates are required.

What fails.

  • The old digest is deleted when the new one starts loading.
  • The canary looks only at error rate.
  • Image, digest, and a timeout change land together.
  • Rollback needs a build because the previous image tag moved.

What you do. Pin image and model by digest. Canary a slice. Abort on latency or errors. Keep the last good pin loadable.

baseline_p95_ms: 200
canary_p95_ms: 260
budget_ms: 220
action: abort

problems.title: Not ready
problems.promptHtml: The process binds a port in 1 second and finishes loading weights in about 6.7 seconds. A balancer uses the open port as readiness. What happens to requests in the first 6 seconds, and what should readiness wait for?
problems.answer: they hit a replica that cannot serve yet; readiness waits for a tiny successful generate.

problems.title: Liveness
problems.promptHtml: Startup takes about 6.7 seconds. Liveness kills the container if it does not answer in 3 seconds. Will the replica ever become ready, and what probe should cover startup?
problems.answer: no, it will be killed during load; a startup probe longer than the load, then liveness.

problems.title: How many replicas
problems.promptHtml: You target 7 requests per second per replica and arrivals are 28 per second. How many ready replicas do you want? Why is a GPU-utilization target a weaker signal for a bandwidth-bound decode?
problems.answer: 4 ready replicas; utilization can look modest while you are already on the latency roof.

problems.title: Spill
problems.promptHtml: Region B has 2 ready replicas, 20 requests per second of capacity, and 40 of nearest-region demand. Region A has spare capacity. How many requests per second should spill to A, and what policy fails to do that?
problems.answer: 20 per second spill; nearest-region routing without a capacity cap overloads B.

problems.title: Abort
problems.promptHtml: Baseline p95 is 200 ms, the budget is 220 ms, and a 5% canary measures 260 ms with no extra errors. Do you continue the rollout, and why are zero errors not enough?
problems.answer: abort; latency missed the budget even though errors stayed flat.

problems.title: Drain
problems.promptHtml: A scale-in hard-kills a replica with 20 in-flight decodes. Those clients retry immediately on the remaining replicas. Why can that cause a second overload, and what should scale-in do instead?
problems.answer: retries pile onto fewer replicas; mark not-ready and drain in-flight work first.

problems.title: Warm floor
problems.promptHtml: Startup is about 6.7 seconds. The product needs a first token within 1 second, including queue. Why can scaling from zero not meet a sudden burst, and what do you keep running when traffic is quiet?
problems.answer: new replicas are not ready for 6.7 seconds, past the 1 second budget; keep a warm floor of ready replicas.

problems.title: One change
problems.promptHtml: A deploy updates the engine image, the model digest, and the client timeout, then p95 improves. Why is the undo unclear, and what should a reversible deploy contain?
problems.answer: three changes moved, so you cannot tell what to revert; one pinned change, with the previous pin still loadable.

bonus.title: Ready capacity
bonus.promptHtml: Desired replicas are 6, ready replicas are 4, each ready replica can take 10 requests per second, and arrivals are 50 per second. Startup of the two new replicas takes about 6.7 seconds. Are you short right now, by how many requests per second, and why does the desired count of 6 not answer the page?
bonus.answer: ready capacity is 40 per second, short by 10; desired replicas are not ready yet, so they add no capacity during startup.

articles.title: The metrics that page
articles.html:
Page on a small set of numbers that mean a user is about to suffer or a GPU is on fire. For chat, that is p95 time to first token, p95 inter-token time, error rate, and queue time, sliced by route and length bucket. Add ready replicas next to desired. Add a quality canary if you can score a trickle of production prompts. Do not page on a hundred gauges. The one that fires should be the one you act on.

A burn alert beats a single spike. You care that the budget is being consumed, not that one request was slow. Tie the alert to the same budget you wrote in the prerequisites chapter.

Mechanism. The server emits histograms for the clocks you named in the stack: gateway, queue, prefill, decode. The client emits its own end-to-end clock, because a timeout the server never saw is still a failure. Alerts look at a percentile over a window, with a minimum number of requests so a quiet night does not page on one outlier. A separate alert fires when ready lags desired for longer than startup. GPU errors, such as a device falling off the bus, page immediately and drain that node. They are not a latency problem to tune through.

Worked numbers. The budget is 220 ms p95 time to first token. Over five minutes you see p95 at 300 ms on the long-prompt bucket and 180 ms on the short-prompt bucket, with 2,000 requests in the window. You page the long bucket. A global p95 of 200 ms would have stayed quiet and hidden the slice. Separately, one node reports a GPU fault. You drain it even if the global p95 is fine, because the next fault will be a user-facing error. The short bucket does not get a kernel rollback. The long bucket might be a prefix-cache miss or a real prefill regression. The slice is what makes that distinction possible.

What fails.

  • One latency alert covers every route and every length.
  • The client timeout is invisible because only the server exports metrics.
  • A single slow request pages the whole team at 3 a.m.
  • A GPU fault is left in rotation while you tune a batch size.

What you do. Alert on sliced percentiles with a minimum volume, on ready lag, and on device faults. Drain a bad node before you retune.

budget_ttft_ms: 220
long_p95_ms: 300
short_p95_ms: 180
action: page long bucket

articles.title: Traces and logs
articles.html:
A trace is one request's path across the clocks. A log is the line you grep when the trace says which replica. You need both. The trace without a replica id cannot be matched to a GPU fault. The log without a request id cannot be matched to the slow call. Sample traces when volume is high, and keep every trace for an error.

Logs should carry the digest, the engine version, the batch size, the sequence length, and whether the prefix cache hit. Those fields turn "it was slow" into the bottleneck sentence from the techniques chapter. A log that only says "request failed" is a restart button.

Mechanism. Propagate a request id from the client through the gateway to the engine. The engine records queue, prefill, decode, cache hit, and the replica id. Logs are structured so a query can group by digest. When two digests are in flight during a canary, you can split latency by digest without a new deploy. Retention has to cover the time it takes a human to notice. A five-minute log buffer does not help a ticket filed the next morning. You do not need infinite logs. You need the fields and the id.

Worked numbers. A slow request shows gateway 30 ms, queue 400 ms, prefill 80 ms, decode 40 ms, cache hit false, replica 17. The GPU was not the problem. The queue was. Replica 17's logs show ready replicas on that node dropped from 1 to 0 for a minute while the process restarted, and the balancer still had it in rotation for part of that minute. The trace and the log agree. A kernel profile of replica 18, which was healthy, would have shown a normal 4.7 ms floor and wasted the afternoon. The request id is what stopped that.

What fails.

  • Traces are sampled at 0% because they "cost too much," including on errors.
  • Logs omit the digest during a canary, so you cannot split the regression.
  • The request id stops at the gateway.
  • Replica ids in traces do not match the names in the GPU fault alert.

What you do. Always trace errors. Sample successes. Log digest, replica, lengths, and cache hit next to the request id. Join the slow trace to the replica before you open a profiler.

queue_ms: 400
prefill_ms: 80
decode_ms: 40
replica: 17
cache_hit: false

articles.title: The client
articles.html:
The client sets the timeout, the retries, and how much of the stream it reads. A timeout shorter than the budget you designed will fail healthy requests and, if it retries, will multiply load. A timeout much longer than the budget will hold slots for dead servers. Retries need a budget of their own: a limited count, jitter, and a backoff, and they should not retry a 400 that will never succeed.

Streaming clients have to read until the server is done or until they decide to cancel. Cancelling has to reach the server, or the replica keeps decoding for a caller who left. That is a slot leak.

Mechanism. Set the client timeout from the same split you wrote down: network, queue, prefill, decode. Retry only idempotent calls, or accept that a retry can double-generate. Use a circuit breaker when the error rate is high, so you stop adding load to a sick fleet. Send the request id you want to see in the trace. On cancel, close the connection and have the server abort the sequence and free the cache. Test this. A client bug that never reads the body will look like a server hang.

Worked numbers. The server p95 for a full answer is about 1.1 s. The client timeout is 1,000 ms, so a large slice of healthy answers fail. Those clients retry once. If 30% of answers exceed 1,000 ms, arrivals of 100 per second become 130 per second of server work, and the extra 30 are the ones already slow. The fleet tips over. Raise the client timeout to something past the p95 you intend to support, say 2,000 ms, and retry only on connection errors, with a cap of one retry. The 30% application-level lateness is a capacity or budget problem, not a retry problem. Retrying it makes it worse.

What fails.

  • Client timeout is below the server's healthy p95, with retries on.
  • Cancels do not free the KV cache.
  • A non-idempotent generate is retried and the user is billed twice.
  • Each service in the chain uses a default timeout that is unrelated to the budget.

What you do. Align the client timeout with the budget, cap retries, and abort server work on cancel. Load-test the cancel path.

server_p95_ms: 1100
client_timeout_ms: 1000
retry_on_slow: no
cancel_frees_cache: yes

articles.title: The on-call hour
articles.html:
The hour has an order. Read the page and name the route and the clock. Check ready replicas and device faults. Split the clock by digest and by length. Open one trace of a slow request and join it to a replica. Then change one thing, or roll back the one thing that already changed. Write the sentence down so the next person does not start over.

Most of this course is that order. The model chapter tells you what the clock should be made of. The hardware chapter tells you which ceiling is real. The software chapter tells you which layer owns it. The techniques chapter tells you not to stack fixes. Production is the discipline of doing one of those per hour, not all of them.

Mechanism. Keep a short note in the incident channel: route, clock, before, after, layer, action. If you cannot fill in "before," you are not ready to act. Rolling back is an action. Draining a node is an action. Raising a batch cap without a before-and-after is not an action you can defend. When the hour ends, the note is the postmortem. You do not need a separate literary form if the note has the numbers.

Worked numbers. The page is long-prompt p95 time to first token, 180 ms to 300 ms, short prompts still 180 ms, ready replicas steady, no GPU fault. The canary digest is at 5% and its slice of the trace shows prefill at 200 ms versus 80 ms on the old digest. You abort the canary, as in the deploy lesson. The long-prompt p95 returns to 190 ms within the window. You changed one pointer. A teammate's proposal to quantize, retune the scheduler, and add a region is a plan for next week, after a benchmark, not a plan for this hour. The note is four lines and the system is back.

What fails.

  • The first action is a kernel rewrite while a canary is in flight.
  • Nobody writes down the before value, so "fixed" cannot be checked.
  • A GPU fault and a latency page are treated as one mystery.
  • The incident channel becomes a list of theories with no clocks.

What you do. Route, clock, slice, trace, one action. Roll back if a change is in flight and the slice points at it. Save the broader ideas for a measured experiment.

route: chat
clock: long_ttft_ms 180 -> 300
layer: canary digest
action: abort rollout

problems.title: Slice the page
problems.promptHtml: Long-prompt p95 time to first token is 300 ms against a 220 ms budget. Short-prompt p95 is 180 ms. There were 2,000 requests in the window. Do you page, and which slice do you open?
problems.answer: yes, page the long-prompt bucket; the short bucket is inside the budget.

problems.title: Queue, not kernel
problems.promptHtml: A trace shows queue 400 ms, prefill 80 ms, decode 40 ms. Where do you look, and why is a kernel profile of a healthy replica the wrong room?
problems.answer: the queue and that replica's readiness; the kernels are not the 400 ms.

problems.title: Retries multiply
problems.promptHtml: Server p95 for a full answer is about 1.1 s. The client times out at 1,000 ms and retries those calls. Why does the retry add load instead of helping?
problems.answer: healthy slow answers fail and run again, so the server does the work twice.

problems.title: Drain the fault
problems.promptHtml: Global p95 is inside budget and one node reports a GPU fault. Why do you drain the node before you touch batch size or quantization?
problems.answer: a device fault becomes user-facing errors; tuning a healthy kernel does not repair the device.

problems.title: Join the id
problems.promptHtml: Traces include a replica id and logs include a request id and a digest. A canary is in flight. What can you compare that a single global p95 cannot?
problems.answer: latency split by digest and by replica, so the canary can be blamed or cleared.

problems.title: Cancel
problems.promptHtml: The client closes the stream and the server keeps decoding and holding KV cache. What does that do to slots, and what should the server do on cancel?
problems.answer: slots and cache leak; abort the sequence and free the cache.

problems.title: One action
problems.promptHtml: Long-prompt prefill on the canary digest is 200 ms versus 80 ms on the old digest. Short prompts are fine. Ready count is steady. List the action for this hour, and name one idea you will not try in the same hour.
problems.answer: abort the canary; do not also quantize, retune the scheduler, or add a region in this hour.

problems.title: Write the note
problems.promptHtml: Before the abort, long-prompt time to first token is 300 ms. After it, 190 ms. The budget is 220 ms. What belongs in the incident note so the next on-call can see that the rollback worked?
problems.answer: the route, the clock, 300 to 190 against a 220 budget, the canary as the layer, and the abort as the action.

bonus.title: The hour, in order
bonus.promptHtml: A page fires. You have ready-replica lag, a GPU fault on one node, a canary digest, and a global p95 that moved. Put the checks in order: device fault, ready versus desired, slice by digest and length, one trace, one action. Why is the kernel profiler last?
bonus.answer: drain the faulted node and account for unready replicas before you blame a digest; then slice and trace; the profiler is last because the trace may show queue or a canary prefill, not a kernel.

problems.title: Stage split
problems.promptHtml: A product change lengthens prompts. Time to first token moves from 90 ms to 640 ms. Time between tokens stays near 30 ms. Which stage regressed, and why is a decode capacity purchase the wrong first buy?
problems.answer: prefill regressed with prompt length; decode inter-token time did not move.

problems.title: Ready count
problems.promptHtml: Arrivals are 60 requests per second. Each ready replica can take 10. Ready replicas are 4 while desired is 6, and the new pods are not ready. What is the shortfall in replicas, and why did the higher desired count not fix it?
problems.answer: shortfall is 2 ready replicas; unready pods add no capacity.

problems.title: Fourteen and fifty-six
problems.promptHtml: A serving disk fills with a 70 GB copy of a 7B training run. BF16 weights are 14 GB. What is the other 56 GB, and which layer are you in if the process cannot even load the file?
problems.answer: optimizer state; the artifact is wrong before runtime tuning matters, so fix the export.

problems.title: Does it fit the timeout
problems.promptHtml: Network and gateway take 40 ms of a 1,000 ms client timeout. First token is budgeted at 200 ms. 80 output tokens remain. What inter-token budget is left, in milliseconds?

problems.title: Frozen bar
problems.promptHtml: INT4 doubles throughput and scores 71. The bar is 80 and the BF16 score was 84. Why does the throughput number not promote the export?
problems.answer: 71 is under the bar by 9 points; speed does not replace the frozen eval.

problems.title: Slots before kernels
problems.promptHtml: You need 50 slots and you have 32. A proposed kernel reduces service time by 10%, from 0.5 s to 0.45 s, at 100 arrivals per second. How many slots do you still need, and do you buy GPUs or the kernel first?
problems.answer: you still need 45 slots and you have 32, so you are 13 short; buy capacity first.

problems.title: Cache at the max
problems.promptHtml: One 2,048-token sequence is about 256 MB of KV cache. Max length is 8,192 and max sequences is 32. About how much cache must the replica be able to hold?
problems.answer: 8,192 / 2,048 = 4, so about 1 GB per sequence and about 32 GB for 32 sequences.

problems.title: Which peak
problems.promptHtml: Math for one decode token would take 0.5 ms. Moving 14 GB at 3,000 GB/s takes about 4.7 ms. Which peak is the step hitting, and what would twice the FLOPs change?
problems.answer: the bandwidth peak; twice the FLOPs would still leave the step near 4.7 ms.

problems.title: Images are steps
problems.promptHtml: A 30-step image at 40 ms per step plus a 50 ms decoder is the whole request. Why is a time-to-first-token chart from chat the wrong page for this route?
problems.answer: the caller waits on the step loop, about 1,200 ms plus the decoder, not on a token stream.

problems.title: Roof
problems.promptHtml: A kernel's bandwidth floor is 4.7 ms and its compute floor is 0.5 ms. The measurement is 5.1 ms. Are you on the roof, and which spec-sheet line is the one that matters?
problems.answer: yes, near the bandwidth roof; HBM bandwidth matters, not peak FLOPs.

problems.title: Cold versus HBM
problems.promptHtml: HBM would read 14 GB in about 4.7 ms. The host path loads the same 14 GB checkpoint in about 4.7 s. Why are those two times not in conflict?
problems.answer: HBM bandwidth is on-GPU traffic during a step; the cold load is a different, slower path into the GPU.

problems.title: Do not split yet
problems.promptHtml: Single-GPU decode floor is 4.7 ms. A two-GPU split would exchange about 3,200 MB on a 400 GB/s link, an 8 ms floor. The model fits on one GPU. What do you do?
problems.answer: stay on one GPU; the link floor is worse than the single-GPU floor.

problems.title: Scheduler before GPUs
problems.promptHtml: Batch-1 serving measures about 200 tokens per second. A batched engine on the same GPU measures about 1,400. Demand is 1,000 tokens per second. How many batch-1 GPUs would you have bought, and how many batched GPUs do you need?
problems.answer: 5 batch-1 GPUs versus one batched GPU.

problems.title: Fallback
problems.promptHtml: A compiled path is 50 ms inside the profile and 120 ms on the fallback. The previous engine was 80 ms for those long prompts. What should you do before you send all traffic to the compiled engine?
problems.answer: keep long prompts off the fallback, or rebuild the profile to include them; 120 ms is a regression.

problems.title: Twice
problems.promptHtml: Baseline p95 is 200 ms and 206 ms. What is the noise band, and why is a candidate at 203 ms not a ship?
problems.answer: about 6 ms; 203 ms sits inside the band between the two baselines.

problems.title: Floor moved
problems.promptHtml: BF16 decode floor is about 4.7 ms. INT8 streams half the bytes. What floor are you aiming at, and what does a measurement still near 4.7 ms mean?
problems.answer: about 2.3 ms; the kernel is still moving the wide weights.

problems.title: One token accepted
problems.promptHtml: Speculation spends 7 ms to verify, accepts no draft tokens, and emits only the replacement, versus a 5 ms plain step. Do you keep it?
problems.answer: no; 7 ms for one token is slower than 5 ms.

problems.title: Network decides
problems.promptHtml: Cache for a sequence is about 256 MB. The shared-GPU stall is 80 ms. At what order of network bandwidth is a 256 MB copy cheaper than that stall? Use 10 GB/s versus 1 GB/s in the answer.
problems.answer: at 10 GB/s the copy is about 26 ms and cheaper; at 1 GB/s it is about 256 ms and not cheaper.

problems.title: Visual tokens
problems.promptHtml: Vision encode is 40 ms and language prefill of the 1,000 visual tokens is 80 ms. Why is a text-only prompt length the wrong size for this time to first token?
problems.answer: the image adds the encoder and about 1,000 tokens, so first token is about 120 ms before decode, not the cost of a short question.

problems.title: Steps that pass
problems.promptHtml: The image eval fails at 10 steps and passes at 20. Each step is 40 ms. What do you ship, and what is the model time?
problems.answer: 20 steps; 800 ms of denoiser time.

problems.title: Own timeout
problems.promptHtml: A video preview needs about 3.5 seconds. Chat is budgeted at 2 seconds. Why does one timeout fail at least one of them no matter which number you pick?
problems.answer: a timeout under 3.5 seconds fails video; a timeout of several seconds makes chat hold slots and retry late; each route needs its own budget.
